## [Study Questions Reliability of Difficulty Labels in RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40115) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.40115) reexamines the 'unlearnability' phenomenon in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), finding that prompts previously labeled unlearnable do improve during training, at roughly one third of the learnable rate. The authors show that difficulty labels estimated from limited sampled responses are far less reproducible than assumed, and they propose a sampling-based framework to quantify this instability. This work matters because many RLVR and post-training studies rely on difficulty labels to select prompts and draw conclusions about what models can or cannot learn; if those labels are unstable, downstream findings may be distorted. It calls for more careful measurement in evaluation and could influence how researchers design RLVR experiments and interpret 'unlearnable' prompts. The paper shows that combining difficulty labels across random seeds can change which prompts are selected rather than simply reducing measurement noise, and it revisits the gradient-similarity evidence for unlearnability, finding that part of the observed separation stems from difficult prompts providing fewer correct rollouts for gradient estimation. Matching the sample count weakens but does not eliminate the gradient difference, so the slow-learning phenomenon survives the reanalysis even as its defining prompts and explanatory evidence require better measurement.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is a post-training approach that improves reasoning by rewarding the model for verifiably correct answers, and it has become prominent through methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization used in DeepSeek-R1. In RLVR research, prompts are often classified as easy, learnable, or unlearnable based on how often a model solves them across a limited number of sampled responses. This paper examines whether those difficulty labels are reliable enough to support claims about which prompts a model fundamentally cannot learn.

## [ScholarEvolve Uses Research Literature to Evolve Agent Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40169) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.40169) introduces ScholarEvolve, a framework that automatically draws on state-of-the-art research literature to guide the evolution of language agent harnesses while keeping the underlying model fixed. It organizes harness evolution into functional modules, uses topic modeling to identify improvement strategies per module, and evaluates their combinations, raising Qwen3.5-27B task goal completion on AppWorld Challenge from 49.6% to 63.6% and GPT-5.4-mini pass@1 on Tau2-Bench Telecom from 72.7% to 81.9%. This shifts agent self-improvement from reactive, failure-driven patching toward proactive, literature-guided evolution, potentially making agents improve continuously without retraining or swapping the base model. It matters for teams building long-running agents, since the harness—not the model—is increasingly seen as the main determinant of agent reliability at scale. The framework is designed to incorporate new publications over time, enabling proactive lifelong evolution, and its gains are demonstrated on two benchmarks (AppWorld and Tau2-Bench) using fixed models. As an arXiv preprint, it has not yet undergone peer review, and no community discussion is available.

**Background**: An agent harness is the runtime scaffolding around a language model that governs tool use, memory management, context handling, and multi-step task execution; a survey of 110+ papers argues the harness, not the model, is the primary determinant of agent reliability at scale. Recent methods use a meta coding agent to modify the harness based on execution feedback, but this relies on the agent's existing knowledge and observed failures, limiting exploration. ## [MAGIC: Belief-Aware MAPF Infers Unobserved Obstacles via Spatial Correlation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40269) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.40269v1) introduces MAGIC (Multi-Agent Gaussian belief Inference for Coordination), a framework for Belief-Aware Multi-Agent Path Finding that maintains a shared online belief about traversability using a Gaussian Markov Random Field and Gaussian Belief Propagation. Experiments on MAPF benchmarks show MAGIC reduces the executed sum of costs compared to existing contingent planning and replanning approaches on 96.3% of instances, across several planner families and teams of up to 800 agents. Classical MAPF assumes all static obstacles are known in advance, which breaks down in real warehouses and other dynamic environments where fallen objects or spills create unexpected blockages. By letting a single observation inform traversability estimates for nearby unobserved locations, MAGIC can anticipate obstacles that would otherwise force costly rerouting, making it relevant for large-scale automated warehouses and robot fleets. MAGIC targets the Belief-Aware MAPF setting where map discrepancies are fixed during execution but initially unknown, and it uses a Gaussian Markov Random Field with Gaussian Belief Propagation to approximately infer traversability and construct detour-aware costs for standard MAPF planners. The approach is approximate rather than exact, and the evaluation is limited to benchmark instances rather than real-world deployments.

## [PivotOPD Teaches Multi-Turn Agents to Prevent and Recover from Pivotal Mistakes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40285) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose PivotOPD, an on-policy distillation framework that jointly trains multi-turn language agents to prevent pivotal mistakes and to recover from the states those mistakes create. Experiments across three Qwen3 models (8B to 235B) show that over half of failed rollouts contain an early pivotal mistake that is often recoverable with a few turns of teacher guidance, and PivotOPD beats 13 baselines on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA, improving ALFWorld by +5.5% with a Qwen3-1.7B student and raising a Nemotron-3.5 student's resolve rate on SWE-Bench Verified by +3.2%. Error compounding is a core obstacle to deploying language agents in long-horizon interactive tasks, since one bad action shifts the agent into states it never learned to handle. By showing that most failures trace back to a small number of early, recoverable pivotal mistakes, this work offers a practical training recipe that could make agents substantially more robust without changing the underlying model architecture. PivotOPD uses two complementary distillation signals: preventive distillation applies reverse KL on the teacher's gold action to steer the student away from the pivotal mistake, while recovery distillation applies forward KL on teacher-named recovery actions to transfer behaviors the student rarely samples on its own. The method is evaluated with Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B students against 13 baselines, and the gains transfer to a different model family (Nemotron-3.5) in the software engineering domain.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on trajectories it generates itself while a stronger teacher provides dense token-level supervision, which is more informative than sparse task rewards. In multi-turn agent settings, however, the student's own incorrect action changes the environment state for all later turns, so a single early mistake can cascade into failure. Pivotal mistakes are defined as actions that move the agent farther from completing the task, and the paper's key observation is that these mistakes are usually early and often recoverable rather than fatal.

## [FairMedAgent exposes instability floor in clinical LLM fairness audits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03221) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces FairMedAgent, a harness that measures the inherent stochastic instability of clinical LLM agents, showing that re-running the same condition ten times over sixteen synthetic vignettes at default sampling changed the agent's action in 8.7% of replicate pairs, with pooled floors across six models ranging from 2.5% to 23.7%. It also demonstrates that majority voting over five draws removes 39% of this floor (95% CI 18–64), and that for a binary action the expected flip rate under no demographic effect equals the floor, meaning a flip rate inside the floor is not evidence of fairness. This work reveals a critical methodological flaw in counterfactual fairness audits of clinical LLM agents: stochastic decoding creates an 'instability floor' that can be mistaken for demographic bias, potentially leading to false conclusions about fairness. It provides a four-step reporting procedure and releases the FairMedAgent harness, which will help researchers and practitioners conduct more accurate fairness evaluations and avoid conflating noise with real bias. The instability floor depends on the decoding configuration: at temperature 0, three of four locally served models showed no disagreement, but a hosted model still did. The paper also shows that for a binary action, the flip rate expected under no demographic effect equals the floor and a real effect adds only its square, so direction must be tested with a signed paired test.

**Background**: Counterfactual fairness audits of clinical language-model agents typically report a flip rate: how often an action changes when only the patient's demographic descriptor changes. The paper addresses this gap by measuring the instability floor and providing a framework to separate noise from true demographic bias.

ModalFidelity introduces a lightweight router that previews each one-second video window and decides, before any forensic detector runs, which stream (audio or image) is worth reading under a hard compute budget. The router operates under a hard compute budget it can never exceed, previewing windows cheaply before committing to a full forensic detector pass. ## [Randomized Audits Can't Deter AI Agents That Erase Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38262) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.38262) analyzes when randomized audits and scoring can align AI agents that can conceal misconduct and alter records. It shows that stronger auditing paradoxically makes undeterred violations better hidden, and that rare audits deter all agent types only if evidence survives concealment and audit draws cannot be learned in advance. The paper offers a formal mechanism-design lens on a central AI safety problem: oversight itself changes the evidence it depends on, so audit regimes can backfire. Its conditions are tied directly to OpenAI's July 2026 cybersecurity evaluation incident, making the theory practically grounded for labs and regulators designing oversight. Because the provider writes the agent's objective, sanctions need not stop at forfeiture, and rare audits suffice when evidence survives concealment and audit timing cannot be anticipated. When evidence can be erased, deterrence must instead come from lowering the gains from violation—such as credit for stopping—or from making concealment costlier or less available.

## [Janus: Evidence-Before-Effect Provenance for Agentic LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38266) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38266) introduces Janus, a system that records an agentic LLM step's proposal, its verdict, and any validator or human answer into a signed, hash-chained log before the step may run or its effect be released. It was evaluated under crash injection (144 in-process kills, 81 through the daemon), by offline verification of a 100-million-event log in 254.5 seconds, and in a lending workflow where Janus blocked all six over-mandate loans that a plain agent paid. Agentic LLMs increasingly move money and take real-world actions through tools, yet their audit trail is typically a trace emitted by the same process that performs the effect, which is insufficient for trustworthy accountability. Janus shifts the record onto the effect path and makes verdicts offline-verifiable from the log plus one public key, a contribution that could influence future standards for auditing autonomous systems. Gates in Janus are pure functions of the log, and at the MCP edge the effect is held until verification completes, while through the SDK a cooperating client runs the effect only afterwards. The paper also reports a post-approval substitution flaw found during experiment design—an approval keyed to one attempt was counted for a different proposal, moving a person's approval from 100 to 1,000,000—along with a first fix, five routes around it, and an explicit statement of what Janus does not guarantee.

A new arXiv paper (2609.38332) introduces Hermes, a family of configurable harnesses that progressively vary how much control a model has over allocating fresh context windows and reusing information across them, plus Hermes-Learn, a two-stage training framework for learning these decisions. The authors report that capable models exploit this flexibility to scale with additional inference-time compute, while smaller open-source models initially struggle until Hermes-Learn training closes the gap. Test-time scaling is one of the most active directions in LLM research now that pretraining compute gains are slowing, and this work shifts context-allocation decisions from hand-designed harnesses to the model itself. If the learned strategies generalize and extrapolate as claimed, it could make inference-time compute more efficient and bring adaptive reasoning within reach of smaller open-source models. The paper defines "contextual reasoning" as a model's ability to decide how to allocate fresh contexts and what information to carry between them, and it reports that the induced strategies vary with both the problem and the progress of reasoning. The authors claim the gains generalize across benchmarks and models, extrapolate beyond the inference-time compute seen during training, and transfer to complementary test-time scaling methods beyond Hermes.

## [Aegis Uses Generative Gradient Masking to Defend Medical Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38339) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Aegis introduces a client-side defense for federated learning that superimposes a masking gradient computed on locally synthesized, task-relevant data onto each client's real update, deliberately pushing the effective batch size beyond the recovery capacity of model inversion attacks. Evaluated on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and three MedMNIST modalities (chest X-ray, abdominal CT, colon pathology), it neutralizes three state-of-the-art MIAs while preserving model utility with only modest overhead. This work breaks the long-standing dilemma in privacy-preserving federated learning where gradient-perturbation defenses sacrifice diagnostic accuracy and cryptographic protocols add system complexity yet still leave updates exposed to scalable attacks. If validated, Aegis could offer hospitals and research centers a practical privacy primitive for multi-institutional medical AI without compromising clinical reliability. Aegis requires no perturbation of patient data and no modification to the FL protocol, and it comes with theoretical convergence guarantees under standard convex assumptions. The defense exploits the observation that every known MIA is fundamentally bounded by the local batch size relative to the model's leakage capacity, so once that limit is exceeded, distinct samples collide and reconstructions collapse into indistinguishable mixtures.

## [OpenCollab: Programmable Multi-Agent Coding with Adherence Metric](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38345) ⭐️ 7.0/10

OpenCollab is a new multi-agent coding framework that unifies programmable collaboration design with a controllable shared runtime, and introduces 'Adherence' to quantify whether the declared agent organization is actually realized during execution. Experiments show Adherence varies from 47.2% to 97.2% across configurations, and a two-coder workflow built on OpenCollab achieves new SOTA results against Mini-SWE-agent, Codex CLI, and Claude Code. Existing multi-agent evaluations assume the configured organization is followed faithfully, so observed gains cannot be cleanly attributed to design versus runtime mechanics; OpenCollab's Adherence metric exposes this behavioral gap and provides a controlled causal evaluation infrastructure. This matters for AI/ML and software engineering researchers building agentic coding systems, since it shows organization design can outperform strong existing harnesses while also revealing that collaboration fidelity is highly configuration-dependent. OpenCollab decouples organization design from execution mechanics, enforces experimental control on a shared runtime, and tracks execution via fine-grained event streams; changing any single dimension shifts Adherence between 47.2% and 97.2%. Its single-agent configuration also uses the fewest tokens across all evaluated suites, though the framework's benefits depend on how faithfully the declared organization is realized.

Researchers introduced MILO (Meta-evolutionary Island Orchestration), a framework that co-evolves agent harnesses together with the search strategy used to discover them, combining hierarchical lineage memory over island-based trees, per-island mutator agents, and an orchestrator that adapts search via lineage grafting and speciation. Across Terminal-Bench 2.1, PaperBench, and DeepSWE, MILO-discovered harnesses beat eight state-of-the-art harnesses and six search methods, improving over its initial harness by +12.0%, +28.3%, and +10.3% with Opus 4.8, and reaching 86.1±2.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, above the official leaderboard's top entry of 83.8±2.3% while using 26% fewer tokens. MILO's ability to outperform both hand-built harnesses and prior automated search methods suggests meta-evolutionary co-evolution is a promising direction for building agentic systems that keep pace with rapidly evolving foundation models. MILO uses rejected mutations as negative evidence in its hierarchical lineage memory, and its orchestrator performs lineage grafting, speciation, mutator reassignment, and curriculum revision to avoid the fixed, exploitative search strategies that trap prior methods. On EinsteinArena open problems it also improved best-known upper bounds for Erdős minimum-overlap (0.3808586 → 0.3808568) and the first and third autocorrelation inequalities (1.50274365 → 1.50274360; 1.45081 → 1.44889), though as a preprint its practical impact remains to be independently validated.

## [SCOUT Fixes Off-Policy Teacher Mismatch in On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38360) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38360) identifies a fundamental asymmetry in on-policy distillation (OPD): while student-generated trajectories are on-policy for the student, they are off-policy for the teacher, whose continuation performance degrades as student prefixes grow longer. To address this, the authors propose SCOUT (Student-COnditioned Updates of the Teacher), a co-training framework that periodically adapts the teacher to student-generated prefixes using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). This work exposes a previously overlooked weakness in OPD, an emerging post-training paradigm for transferring capabilities from large teachers to smaller students, and offers a concrete mechanism to fix it. If validated, SCOUT could improve distillation effectiveness across model scales and reasoning domains, making it directly relevant to researchers and engineers building efficient deployable LLMs. SCOUT alternates standard OPD updates with periodic teacher optimization: the teacher generates continuations from student prefixes and learns from outcome rewards via RLVR. Controlled experiments show improved teacher continuation on student prefixes, and consistent OPD gains across multiple teacher-student configurations, model scales, and reasoning domains.

**Background**: Knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller student model, traditionally by training the student to imitate teacher-generated text. On-policy distillation (OPD) instead has the student sample its own trajectories while the teacher provides dense token-level supervision, combining the state alignment of on-policy RL with the dense feedback of distillation. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a post-training method where rewards come from automatic, rule-based checkers rather than learned reward models or human raters.

The paper proposes Simulator-Refined Diffusion (SRD), which combines a low-fidelity differentiable surrogate with a high-fidelity non-differentiable electromagnetic simulator during diffusion sampling to generate PCB layouts matching target S-parameters. Experiments show SRD outperforms state-of-the-art methods, matching target specifications up to 21.2% closer for in-distribution targets and 19.8% for out-of-distribution targets. This addresses a key bottleneck in AI-driven hardware design: diffusion models can generate layouts but struggle to meet quantitative electromagnetic specs, and full-wave simulators are accurate yet expensive and non-differentiable. SRD offers a practical way to bridge generative AI with rigorous simulation, potentially speeding up RF and PCB design cycles. Unlike standard zeroth-order optimization that needs many random perturbations, SRD uses the surrogate's gradient to propose a perturbation direction, and the high-fidelity simulator then searches along that direction to find an effective design update. The method is evaluated across different settings and consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches.

A new arXiv paper (2609.38364) introduces the Discrete Average Generator, which extends the MeanFlow framework from continuous spaces to Continuous-Time Markov Chains (CTMCs) by defining an average generator as the normalized increment of the transition kernel over a time interval. The authors derive a self-consistency identity that yields a tractable training objective, reporting up to 67% reduction in total variation distance for the K-step sampler in Potts model simulations, the lowest generative perplexity among evaluated methods on OpenWebText for 8 to 64 sampling steps with 16x acceleration, and comparable performance to existing methods on ImageNet. If the reported 16x speedup and perplexity gains hold up, the method could influence how future discrete diffusion language models are trained and sampled. The key technical insight is that when the self-consistency identity is projected onto per-coordinate marginals, it admits a closed-form expression, which is what makes both training and inference efficient. The training strategies are designed to align with the standard training paradigm of diffusion language models, and the evaluation spans Potts model simulations, OpenWebText text generation, and ImageNet image generation, though the work is a preprint without peer review or community engagement metrics yet.

A new arXiv paper (2609.38420) introduces Type-6 logic, a variant of dynamic epistemic logic augmented with uncertainty and recurrence operators, to formally model the inferential dynamics of LLM chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. The authors build a verifier that constructs a graph from the reasoning trace and checks it against Type-6 axioms and inference rules, detecting structurally unsound steps that surface-level heuristics miss. The framework addresses a critical need for trustworthy AI by offering a formal, provably efficient method to verify CoT reasoning, which could significantly impact AI safety and interpretability. It also shows that existing verification methods such as LLMs-as-judges and LINC are not interchangeable, with agreement as low as κ ≈ 0.034, suggesting the field needs more rigorous standards. The verifier runs in average-case linear time, and evaluation on four splits spanning formal and informal reasoning shows derived contradiction is the most common hard-fail category, while only about 3% of trace propositions actually impact the final derivation. Type-6 was the most agreed-with method among those tested, and the authors release the logic specification and artifacts.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Dynamic epistemic logic (DEL) is a formal framework for reasoning about how knowledge and information change when events occur, often used in multi-agent systems and AI. Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting encourages LLMs to produce step-by-step reasoning, but these traces can contain unlicensed revisions, enthymemes (arguments with unstated premises), loopbacks, and unverifiable claims. Type-6 logic extends DEL with operators for uncertainty and recurrence to capture these pathologies and enable automated verification of reasoning traces.

## [TACIT Uses LLMs to Repair Misspecified Optimization Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38434) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TACIT, a new method described in arXiv paper 2609.38434, automatically repairs misspecified optimization formulations by combining LLM reasoning with formal optimization, using historical solutions and user overrides as training signals. Evaluated on 38 misspecification scenarios across nine classes of optimization problems, it repaired 78.9% of them, compared with 60.5% for the best baseline. Misspecified optimization models are a persistent and costly problem in operations research, since objectives and constraints often live in domain experts' tacit knowledge. TACIT's ability to learn from user overrides and produce interpretable repairs could reduce manual model maintenance and make optimization tools more reliable in real-world deployment. TACIT combines two complementary paradigms: a top-down approach where an LLM proposes structural repairs such as new constraints and variables whose parameters are calibrated and validated through optimization, and a bottom-up approach where optimization infers cuts from observed decisions that the LLM contextualizes into interpretable, generalizable constraints. The evaluation spans 38 misspecification scenarios across nine problem classes, several drawn from real-world applications.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Mathematical optimization seeks optimal decisions under given objectives and constraints, but real-world models often contain miscalibrated objectives, missing constraints, or omitted decision variables because expert knowledge is hard to formalize. Traditional repair approaches such as inverse optimization and constraint learning infer models from observed decisions but tend to overfit sparse data and produce overly complex formulations. TACIT instead leverages LLMs' prior knowledge and reasoning alongside formal optimization grounding to produce simpler, more generalizable repairs.

## [Study Explains How Pretraining and Midtraining Enable Reward Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38446) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38446) theoretically and empirically investigates how pretraining and midtraining supply the information and computation needed for effective reward adaptation. Using Qwen2.5 checkpoints across eight synthetic worlds, the authors show that models trained with correct source and first-operation supervision reach 82.61% success versus 44.15% for a private-random source control, and that memory replay preserves retrieval during reward adaptation. The findings clarify the division of labor between source prediction (which acquires execution or retrieval capabilities) and reward adaptation (which learns task-specific use), offering a principled account of why pretraining and midtraining matter for reinforcement-learning-based post-training. This could inform how practitioners design data mixtures and intermediate training stages for reward-driven fine-tuning of large language models. The paper constructs finite sampled Adam paths from specified random initializations through source prediction and reward adaptation in the same parameters, proving how prediction acquires execution or retrieval while rewards learn their task-specific use. An independent eight-world confirmation achieves 75.32% task success versus 49.86% after matched alternative-retrieval training, and GSM8K and HotpotQA separate accuracy at reward entry, subsequent gain, and final performance.

**Background**: Pretraining is the large-scale phase where a language model learns broad linguistic and semantic features from trillions of web tokens, while midtraining (also called continued pretraining) is an intermediate stage that refines data mixtures, extends context length, and builds domain expertise before task-specific fine-tuning. Reward adaptation in reinforcement learning refers to adapting an agent to a target reward function based on source behaviors learned under the same dynamics but different rewards. This paper asks what information and computation these stages must supply so that reward signals can actually guide learning.

## [Gradient Conflict Metrics Fail to Predict Understanding-Generation Trade-off in Unified Multimodal Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38465) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A controlled audit using the GRIDUMM testbed, spanning 63 configurations and 372 checkpoints, found that no directional gradient conflict metric achieves an absolute Spearman correlation of 0.3 with the eventual understanding-generation trade-off. A dose-response intervention that monotonically suppresses conflict left the trade-off flat, separating correlation from causation. This negative result challenges a widely held design premise in unified multimodal models, suggesting that research efforts directed at minimizing gradient conflict metrics may be misallocated. It calls for establishing the validity of diagnostic targets rather than assuming them, and releases a reusable audit protocol. The norm ratio acts as a generation-failure detector and becomes null among configurations that master generation, while functional interference measures outperform directional conflict metrics and training loss tracks the trade-off strongly. The audit protocol is released as a reusable standard.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) aim to handle both understanding (e.g., image captioning) and generation (e.g., text-to-image) within a single architecture, but these objectives often conflict, creating a trade-off where improving one degrades the other. Gradient conflict metrics, which measure opposing gradient directions between tasks, are commonly used to diagnose and mitigate this trade-off, but their predictive validity had not been directly tested.

## [BACKDROP benchmark shows agent pass rates collapse from 69.5% to 31.3% under four everyday hazards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38469) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced BACKDROP, a benchmark that takes an agent's task and execution environment and plants four everyday hazards — authority, injection, boundary, and fault — one at a time and all together, while keeping the instruction and correct end state unchanged. Across 3,678 variants and 16 models, the average pass rate fell from 69.5% in a clean world to 31.3% with all four hazards present, with the strongest models dropping the most (Claude Fable 5.1 from 96.6% to 56.0%). Most agent benchmarks test agents in worlds that stay still, but deployed agents operate in environments that other people also change, so this work exposes a large gap between clean-world scores and real-world reliability. The finding that an agent's score in a task's world is effectively a ceiling on real-world performance has direct implications for anyone deploying tool-using agents in production. Counting only runs where the planted text actually reached the agent, agents followed another person's message in 46.4% of runs and injected text in 20.3%, and this gap was consistent across all 16 models. Notably, agents have learned to resist injected text but often still follow other unauthorized requests from other people, suggesting authority confusion is the harder unsolved problem.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: AI agents are systems that use tools, hold credentials, and take multi-step actions on a user's behalf, which makes them vulnerable to prompt injection — text planted in a record or message that redirects the agent — and to authority confusion, where the agent treats attacker-influenced content as sufficient justification for a side-effecting action. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate agents in static environments, so they may overstate how well agents behave when other actors change the world mid-task. BACKDROP formalizes these failure modes by planting hazards in the environment rather than changing the task itself.

## [Controlled Comparison of Six RAG Retrieval Strategies for Scientific QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38473) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38473) presents a controlled comparison of six retrieval strategies for scientific question answering, including classic top-k dense retrieval, LLM-based query rephrasing, rephrasing plus LLM reranking, multi-query fusion via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), an agentic tool-call pipeline, and late-interaction retrieval with ColBERTv2. All pipelines share the same generator (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), prompt, and evaluation protocol, and retrieve from a corpus of 463,971 arXiv papers dated 2024-2025, with a released synthetic dataset of 19,484 questions. The study provides a reproducible, open testbed for understanding cost-quality trade-offs in RAG design choices on a large research-literature corpus, offering practical guidance for practitioners building retrieval-augmented generation systems. It also establishes a basis for future work on faithfulness, retrieval robustness, and agentic retrieval. The five single-vector pipelines share SPECTER2 embeddings and a Chroma vector store, while ColBERTv2 uses late interaction with token-level multi-vector representations. Evaluation uses an LLM-as-a-judge protocol across multiple quality dimensions plus direct gold-paper retrieval metrics, and the synthetic question dataset was generated by Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct from 10,000 randomly sampled papers (query generation succeeded for 9,742).

## [Caption-Mediated Perceived-Safety Estimation for Pedestrian Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38479) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces an explainable pedestrian routing pipeline in which a vision-language model generates a natural-language caption of street-level imagery before any scoring occurs, and perceived-risk classes are derived entirely from structured features of that stored text. Nine captioning conditions across five model families were benchmarked against a direct CLIP image-embedding baseline under an identical downstream pipeline, reaching parity rather than trailing it, and the method was deployed over 654,115 images covering 36 electoral wards in Manchester and Huddersfield. This work shows that an inspectable natural-language intermediate representation can match the accuracy of opaque image embeddings for perceived-safety estimation, which matters for urban planning and pedestrian routing where transparency and public trust are essential. It also provides a rare large-scale field validation, revealing that benchmark gains do not necessarily translate into real-world improvements. Independent field validation against 3,669 locally collected ratings of 494 images across 70 participant sessions found statistically significant but modest agreement at r=0.262, against a measured noise ceiling of 0.737 from rater disagreement; a single-use confirmatory test showed that a pipeline 44% stronger on the supervised benchmark produced no measurable field improvement (r=0.250, p=0.84). Routing behaviour varies with journey length, with negligible change below 1 km and a median 12.78% increase in low-risk route length for a median detour of 2.73% on journeys of 3 to 6 km.

**Background**: CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) is a technique that trains paired image and text encoders with a contrastive objective, enabling zero-shot image-text matching and widely used as a baseline for visual representation. Researchers introduced KlinikeBench, a benchmark of 333 clinician-authored tasks in which a language model must interview a virtual patient, request examinations, follow action constraints, and record a diagnosis within a fixed turn budget. More than 35 clinicians contributed to case authoring and evaluation, and across 31 models from seven families the best systems solved under 30% of tasks despite reaching 90.7% diagnostic accuracy. This work exposes a large gap between static diagnostic accuracy and actual performance during interactive clinical assessment, showing that high scores on chart-based diagnosis benchmarks do not guarantee competent patient interaction. Notably, clinicians rated simulated dialogues higher in mean quality than reference conversations adapted from real conversations, and some models benefit from talking with the patient while others diagnose well from a complete chart but perform much worse in conversation.

## [PANDA: Decentralized Architecture for Scalable, Fault-Tolerant Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38482) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint introduces PANDA, a decentralized architecture for LLM-based multi-agent systems that lets a large collective of heterogeneous, independently administered agents discover each other's capabilities and self-organize into small specialized teams per task. Evaluated on the HotPotQA benchmark, PANDA scales to thousands of agents, assembles teams in milliseconds, matches state-of-the-art accuracy at up to 8x the efficiency, and sustains 100% task completion under faults where existing systems fail. Existing LLM-based multi-agent architectures struggle to support large numbers of agents and concurrent tasks, tolerate failures, govern interactions, and accommodate diverse planning patterns, so PANDA's decoupled design could make large-scale agent collectives practical for real-world deployment. If its claims hold, this work could shift multi-agent system design away from centralized orchestrators toward self-organizing, fault-tolerant collectives. PANDA decouples collective communication from team communication, allowing agents to join multiple teams simultaneously, load-balance tasks across the collective, and schedule concurrent work within each agent. It separates the underlying architecture from the orchestration strategy, supporting three selectable planning and execution patterns (star, chain, and mesh), and uses a web-of-trust model to govern agent interactions without a centralized service that would limit scalability.

Researchers introduced STAM, a state-transition-aware memory framework for clinical LLM agents that records patient state changes as new clinical entries arrive, splitting information into Active (current) and History (superseded or resolved) stores. It combines semantic retrieval with typed clinical relations to identify affected memories, and uses a query-dependent gate to selectively serve historical memory at read time, evaluated across four longitudinal clinical benchmarks. Longitudinal clinical reasoning requires agents to know which patient information still applies while preserving the history needed to reconstruct treatment trajectories, a challenge that simple memory accumulation or overwriting fails to solve. STAM's approach could improve clinical AI reliability and inform general memory management strategies for LLM agents operating over evolving data. STAM maintains current information in an Active store and superseded or resolved information in a History store, using typed clinical relations to identify which memories are affected by new entries. Evaluation included downstream question answering, direct state-maintenance diagnostics, and comparisons at approximately matched context lengths across four longitudinal clinical benchmarks.

## [Study Finds Three Architectural Tensions in AI-Enabled Simulink Controllers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38504) ⭐️ 7.0/10

An empirical study of 62 real-world Simulink models across 8 controller types and 10 application domains, plus a survey of 13 practitioners, identifies three architectural tensions between traditional and AI-enabled controllers. It finds that subsystem organization occupies 68-72% of controller footprint in both paradigms, AI-enabled designs rely heavily on discrete dynamics and user-defined abstraction, and constraint enforcement blocks largely disappear from AI-enabled models. The findings expose a gap between how AI-enabled controller architectures are described in the literature and how they are actually implemented, which matters for researchers and practitioners building AI components into cyber-physical systems. The disappearance of explicit constraint enforcement blocks suggests safety mechanisms are shifting into implicit training-time artifacts, potentially breaking traceability and safety assurance. The study is guided by a literature-derived taxonomy of ten structural categories and nine functional roles, and it notes that discrete dynamics and user-defined abstraction are categories largely absent from AI literature. The authors frame the loss of constraint enforcement blocks as a misalignment between practitioner expectations and actual model structure.

Cyber-physical systems (CPS) combine physical processes with computation and networking, and AI-enabled control increasingly replaces analytically derived control laws in these systems. ## [LLMs Fail at Recursive Social Improvement, Study Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38516) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38516) introduces the concept of 'recursive social improvement,' testing whether self-improving LLM agents can learn from one another to improve an entire population. In controlled experiments, three tested LLMs failed to outperform solo learners, earning less reward per token due to narrow exploration or exhausting their token budget before acting. This counterintuitive negative result challenges the assumption that multi-agent LLM populations naturally benefit from peer learning, which is central to current research on self-improvement and multi-agent systems. It suggests that simply letting agents copy each other may concentrate the population around fewer discoveries rather than expanding collective capability. The study shares a single token budget across independent search, peer learning, and acting, and finds that observing peers helps one model find useful skills sooner and another spend less on private search, but neither outperforms independent learners at equal cost. Skills are copied, revised, and passed on, yet these exchanges concentrate the population around fewer independent discoveries.

**Background**: Recursive self-improvement refers to AI systems rewriting their own code or instructions to become more capable, a long-hypothesized path toward rapid capability gains. Social learning, in contrast, is the idea that agents can acquire skills by observing and copying others rather than discovering everything independently. This paper combines the two ideas, asking whether self-improving LLM agents that each pursue their own reward can collectively lift the whole population through imitation and revision of shared skill files.

ShamAN-Q is a new sub-1-bit post-training quantization method that extends NanoQuant by replacing its diagonal reconstruction geometry with a dense Kronecker-factored curvature metric inspired by the Shampoo optimizer. On Qwen3-Base, it lowers WikiText-2 perplexity at approximately 1 bit-per-weight from 27.56 to 22.96 for the 0.6B model, 19.21 to 16.72 for 1.7B, and 14.29 to 13.80 for 4B, while matching or improving zero-shot accuracy on the Eleuther LM Evaluation Harness. This work pushes the frontier of extreme low-bit LLM compression, potentially enabling large models to run on consumer hardware with less memory and better accuracy. It matters for deployment engineers and researchers seeking to fit ever-larger models into constrained GPU or edge environments. ShamAN-Q fits a Kronecker product to the empirical Fisher information matrix of a small calibration set via Kullback-Leibler minimization, turning NanoQuant's continuous ADMM updates into Sylvester equation solutions while keeping its discrete projection and deployment format unchanged. It also re-measures input curvature per layer before factorization, periodically refreshes statistics on the partially quantized model, and redistributes NanoQuant's uniform rank across layers at the same total bit budget.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses already-trained LLMs by reducing weight precision without retraining, and sub-1-bit methods push this below one bit per weight for extreme memory savings. NanoQuant, from Samsung Labs, was the first PTQ method to reach binary and sub-1-bit levels by formulating quantization as a low-rank binary factorization solved with ADMM. Shampoo is a structure-aware optimizer that approximates second-order curvature using Kronecker-factored covariance, and ShamAN-Q borrows this idea to build a more accurate reconstruction loss.

## [New scaling law unifies data size and KL budget in reward optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38526) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38526) derives a scaling law showing that reward optimization performance scales as Θ(√(min{log(M), K})), where M is the number of preference comparisons and K is the KL-divergence budget. The authors prove this bound information-theoretically and validate it empirically with a 70B gold reward model and proxy models from 0.6B to 4B, achieving R² of 97%–99%. This work fills a gap in AI alignment research by jointly characterizing how training data size and optimization effort affect over-optimization and reward hacking, which are critical failure modes in RLHF. It offers a unified, theoretically grounded view that could guide more efficient data collection and safer optimization budgets for large language models. The scaling law is proven tightly achievable via a constructive procedure and remains robust across model sizes, noise levels, and optimization methods such as best-of-N and policy tilting. The authors suggest reward optimization resembles a simple selection task: choosing from IID Gaussian random variables using noisy preference feedback.

## [Reverse Scoring Fixes Retry Loops in Diffusion Language Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38536) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38536) by Jiacheng Qiu and colleagues identifies why diffusion-based large language model (dLLM) agents get stuck in retry loops: masked decoding's confidence-based commitment causes the sampler to re-commit the failed action because the context already offers a confident fill for the deferred decision. The authors propose a training-free method called Reflect Reverse, which scores candidate actions via the reverse conditional (the likelihood of the task given the state and a candidate action) and improves task success and progression rates over forward-scoring baselines on four multi-turn embodied benchmarks. This work offers a mechanistic explanation for a specific failure mode in diffusion-based LLM agents and a practical, training-free remedy, which could influence future agent design in embodied AI. As dLLMs promise to break the sequential latency bottleneck of autoregressive agents, understanding and fixing their reliability issues is critical for their adoption in real-world agentic tasks. The paper models the distortion of the action distribution as a task-blind corruption, where contextually salient actions (e.g., the action just taken) receive inflated probability by a factor that depends on the state and action but not on the task. Under this model, the task-blind factor cancels exactly from the reverse conditional, which coincides with the task posterior of an idealized uncorrupted model; masked dLLMs can evaluate this reverse conditional natively by masking task tokens and denoising, at the cost of a few parallel passes per candidate.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens in parallel, unlike autoregressive models that generate one token at a time. Masked decoding commits the positions the sampler is most confident about and defers uncertain ones, which can lead to retry loops in embodied agents where a failed action is re-issued because the context provides a confident fill for the deferred decision. This paper builds on the emerging field of diffusion language models and embodied AI, where agents must interact with environments over multiple turns.

## [ReLaG: Scalable Relation-Aware Data Splitting via Proximity Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38538) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced ReLaG, a modality-agnostic framework that models sample relatedness through a hierarchical latent-variable process and infers groups of related samples using proximity graphs and community detection to produce independent train-test splits. Across molecular and protein datasets, ReLaG matches existing relation-aware methods while scaling substantially better, and it adds a label-free procedure for adapting splitting resolution to production data plus a cheap estimate of effective dataset size. Random splits can leak information between train and test sets when samples are related, producing overly optimistic generalization estimates that mislead model selection and deployment decisions. ReLaG's ability to scale relation-aware splitting to previously impractical dataset sizes makes more realistic evaluation feasible in domains like biochemistry, where related samples are common. ReLaG is modality-agnostic, open source, and installable via pip install relag; its inferred groups also yield a cheap estimate of effective dataset size for diversity-aware scaling. The label-free procedure adapts the splitting resolution to production data so that evaluation aligns with the intended deployment setting.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: In machine learning, datasets are typically split randomly into training and test subsets, but this assumes samples are independent. In fields such as biochemical studies, samples often come in related clusters (e.g., similar molecules or protein families), so random splitting can place near-duplicates in both subsets and inflate performance estimates. Relation-aware or group-aware splitting addresses this by keeping related samples together, but existing methods often do not scale to large datasets. Proximity graphs represent data points as vertices with edges encoding similarity, and community detection algorithms partition such graphs into densely connected groups, which ReLaG uses to identify related samples.

## [BaryFM: Flow Matching Model Approximates the Entire Wasserstein Simplex](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38547) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose BaryFM, a flow matching model that transports marginal measures into any Wasserstein barycenter over the simplex, solving what they call Universal Barycenter Approximation. Once trained, the network samples from any barycenter via an ODE and achieves the best average rank among 15 competing methods across 10 domain adaptation benchmarks. Most existing methods compute a barycenter only for a fixed weight vector, so approximating the whole family over the simplex has been underexplored. BaryFM's universal approach could simplify and accelerate applications in domain adaptation, Bayesian posterior aggregation, and algorithmic fairness, where many different weightings may be needed at once. BaryFM is validated on four downstream tasks—domain adaptation, generalization, Bayesian posterior aggregation, and algorithmic fairness—matching or surpassing non-universal solvers. Its key technical mechanism is a flow matching model that learns a vector field whose ODE transports marginal measures into any barycenter in the Wasserstein simplex.

A new arXiv paper introduces FlexRouter, a routing framework that models model complementarity using Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs) and optimizes for answer coverage rather than independently scoring models. It formulates routing as a coverage-oriented subset selection problem, trains via marginalizing over failure sets, and uses a greedy marginal log-determinant strategy at inference to adaptively choose subset sizes without a fixed budget. It introduces the notion of marginal quasi-equivalence and proves that global score minimizers are consistent up to this equivalence under algebraic faithfulness, structural minimality, and model-overlap assumptions. The improved upper bound Õ((K-A)/√(KA) · √T) is established via a sharper analysis of existing sub-sampling algorithms, and the matching lower bound holds up to logarithmic factors, indicating the rate is nearly minimax-optimal. A notable caveat is the requirement that the number of optimal arms A be known up to Õ(1) factors, since near-optimal algorithms for one value of A must incur substantially larger regret for a smaller number of optimal arms.

## [SMART: Self-Evolving Multi-Agent System for Long-Form Subtitle Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38660) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose SMART, a self-evolving multi-agent system that builds persistent series-level memory during test-time training and uses a dynamic router, a Mixture-of-Agents layer, and a judge-refiner loop to adapt agent prompts and routing policies without retraining the underlying LLMs. They also introduce Subtitle Arena (14 genres, 2–198 episodes per series, production years 1959–2023, 15 target locales) and SubMQM, a subtitle-adapted MQM framework with seven dimensions and 19 error categories; SMART achieves the best overall MQM score in all 15 directions, reducing average penalty by 6.9% over the strongest competing agent system, and scores 4.50/5 on the public MuSC benchmark. SMART's test-time training translates only a subset of sentences to evolve the configuration, then applies the evolved setup to the rest of the series; the judge-refiner loop scores candidates and uses textual critiques to update prompts and routing policies without retraining the base LLMs. Evaluation relies on the new Subtitle Arena and SubMQM benchmarks, and the reported 6.9% average penalty reduction and 4.50/5 human-evaluation score are specific to these setups, so generalization to other domains remains to be tested.

## [CollabFlow: Recursive Self-Improvement for LLM Agent Teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38662) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CollabFlow introduces a recursive self-improvement (RSI) system for LLM-based multi-agent collaboration, in which a trainable Collab-Director constructs teams of complete agents, a frozen executor runs them, and each round's outcomes retrain the director. It adds Evidence-Conditioned Communication, where a receiver adopts a differing answer only when the sender's evidence is stronger by a margin, plus a flow-based objective called Collaborative Trajectory Balance (CTB) that keeps several good teams in play; on twelve datasets it outperforms all baselines and keeps improving across rounds. Most existing multi-agent LLM systems leave the collaboration loop open, with pre-defined operator-level collaboration and topology-only learning that propagates errors through verbatim exchanges. By making team construction and communication protocols themselves learnable and by targeting a reward-proportional distribution over teams, CollabFlow points toward self-improving agent ecosystems that could affect how future multi-agent research and production systems are designed. The paper reports that the self-generated target distribution is bounded in how far it can move between rounds, and this bound shrinks as records accumulate. The code is released anonymously at an anonymous.4open.science repository, and the work is an arXiv preprint (2609.38662v1) that has not yet undergone peer review.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) describes a system that improves its own capacity to improve, so each gain makes the next gain easier; in LLM-based multi-agent systems, agents refine one another within a task and outcomes can improve how they collaborate across tasks. Multi-agent LLM systems (MAS) coordinate groups of specialized language models to solve complex tasks collectively, but common designs fix collaboration at the operator level or learn only the communication topology. Evidence-conditioned decision-making ties outputs to explicit evidence to ensure traceability and constrained decisions, which is the idea CollabFlow adapts to inter-agent communication.

## [Theory Explains Why On-Policy Distillation Helps and Hurts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38666) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38666) theoretically analyzes sequential distillation from multiple teachers, showing that forward KL divergence produces a weighted arithmetic mixture of teacher distributions while reverse KL produces a normalized weighted geometric aggregate. The authors develop algorithms that learn these targets under off-policy and on-policy feedback respectively, and establish logarithmic regret bounds in the tabular setting, extending the analysis to function approximation. This work gives a rigorous theoretical foundation for the empirical observation that on-policy distillation (OPD) reduces forgetting compared to supervised fine-tuning, while also explaining its fragility. It could guide researchers and practitioners in choosing between on-policy and off-policy distillation and in designing more robust distillation objectives for large language models. The analysis shows that reverse KL better retains a confident expert's preferences under uninformative feedback, but is more sensitive to teachers that assign very low probabilities to correct responses. Its token-level conditionals also reveal a dependence on continuation distributions that can favor incorrect prefixes over long horizons.

**Background**: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model. In off-policy distillation, the student learns from teacher-generated data via supervised fine-tuning, while in on-policy distillation the student generates its own responses and receives teacher feedback on them. KL divergence measures the difference between two probability distributions and is asymmetric: forward KL is mass-covering, whereas reverse KL is mode-seeking. Regret bounds quantify how much worse an online learning algorithm performs compared to the best possible strategy in hindsight.

## [Always-On Experimentation: Sequential FDR Control via Testing by Betting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38695) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38695) formalizes the "Always-On" experimental setting, where treatments are dynamically generated, added to, and removed from a continuously running experiment, and develops sequential tests that control the false discovery rate (FDR) under arbitrary stopping times and predictable treatment schedules. The approach builds on the testing-by-betting framework, constructing test supermartingales for each treatment's average treatment effect that are shown to be growth-rate optimal in an almost-sure sense. Generative AI has dramatically accelerated how quickly new treatments—from pharmaceuticals to online marketing campaigns—can be conceived and deployed, so modern experimentation platforms increasingly run continuously rather than as fixed-horizon A/B tests. This work provides a principled statistical foundation for deciding which treatments to accept or reject in such always-on pipelines while controlling false discoveries, which matters for platform operators, online experimenters, and statisticians working on sequential and multiple-testing problems. The method achieves time-uniform Type-I error control under arbitrary stopping times and "predictable" treatment schedules, meaning the decision to add or remove treatments cannot depend on future data. The core technical contribution is the construction of test supermartingales for each treatment's average treatment effect, with an almost-sure growth-rate optimality guarantee; the paper is a preprint with no peer review or community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Testing by betting is a sequential, game-theoretic framework that recasts hypothesis testing as a betting game: a bettor accumulates wealth by betting against the null hypothesis, and the resulting nonnegative martingale (or supermartingale) yields anytime-valid evidence, avoiding the limitations of fixed-sample p-values. The false discovery rate (FDR) is the expected proportion of rejected null hypotheses that are actually true, a standard criterion in multiple testing introduced by Benjamini and Hochberg in 1995. A test supermartingale is a nonnegative stochastic process with nonincreasing conditional expectation, whose inverse supremum gives a p-value valid at any stopping time.

## [dattri-LLM: A Unified Library for Training Data Attribution at LLM Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38767) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers released dattri-LLM, a training data attribution (TDA) library that makes gradient-based attribution practical at LLM scale through compact gradient representations and a cost-model-driven dynamic routing of gradient operations. On identical hardware and workloads it achieves 3.2x the throughput of the fastest competing library on average and scales multiple attribution methods to 110B-parameter models across four H200 GPUs. Training data attribution is increasingly important for auditing model behavior, tracing outputs back to training examples, and detecting unauthorized data use, but per-example gradient computation has been prohibitively expensive at LLM scale. By delivering a 3.2x throughput gain and compatibility with existing training loops, dattri-LLM lowers the barrier for researchers and practitioners to apply influence functions and related methods to real large-scale training pipelines. The library's capture mechanism collects per-example gradients from existing training loops that call backward() without modifying the loop or its configuration, supporting distributed training with DDP and FSDP as well as pipelines built on HuggingFace Transformers, TRL, and OLMo. It exposes reusable gradient operations and training-time callbacks that support gradient similarity, curvature-based influence, and trajectory-based methods, plus applications such as online data selection.

## [RPF Dynamics Reframe Forgetting as a Selection Mechanism in Neural Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38768) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.38768) introduces Repeated Reinforcement with Persistent Forgetting (RPF) dynamics, a minimal theoretical framework in which repeated exposure reinforces recurring patterns while persistent forgetting attenuates learned information. The authors derive an exposure-selective survival law, a support-dependent retention boundary, and show that forgetting induces spectral filtering over covariance modes, yielding Minimum Description Length (MDL)-like compression under small-step approximations. This work reframes forgetting from a mere failure mode into a controllable source of inductive bias, potentially offering a new theoretical lens for understanding how neural networks select and retain structure beyond architecture and scale. It could influence how researchers think about training dynamics, regularization, and memory in both biological and artificial learning systems. The theory is built in three layers: an independent-feature model yielding an exposure-selective survival law, a shared-parameter model showing spectral filtering over covariance modes, and a small-step/norm-coding approximation linking RPF to MDL-like compression. Controlled experiments in scalar memories and a nonlinear shared network confirm that joint reinforcement and attenuation interventions shift conditional retention, and that reinforcement timing effects depend on forgetting.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Neural networks are known to exhibit implicit biases such as spectral bias, where they learn low-frequency functions before high-frequency ones, and memorization dynamics that favor simple patterns. Forgetting is typically studied as a problem (e.g., catastrophic forgetting), but this paper treats it as an active selection mechanism. The framework connects to information-theoretic ideas like Minimum Description Length, which balances data fit against model complexity.

## [TID and TIDE: Efficient Training Data Attribution for Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38776) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces TID (Training-data Influence via score Discrepancy), which formulates attribution directly as a local score discrepancy measure applicable to DDPM, EDM, and flow matching, and shows it can be estimated without retraining as a preconditioned gradient similarity using Kronecker-factored curvature. It then distills TID into TIDE, a forward-only student model trained online to reproduce the teacher's rankings from the diffusion model's internal activations, achieving four to five orders of magnitude lower per-query cost. Training data attribution is crucial for understanding which training samples influence generated outputs, with applications in copyright, data valuation, and model debugging, but existing methods are prohibitively expensive. By eliminating costly per-sample gradients and retraining, TID and TIDE make attribution practical at millisecond speeds, potentially enabling real-world adoption in generative AI pipelines. TID uses Kronecker-factored curvature to avoid random projections and per-sample gradient storage, and under counterfactual evaluation on CIFAR-10, ArtBench-10, and MS-COCO it matches or outperforms state-of-the-art approaches. TIDE retains most of TID's accuracy while attributing generated samples in milliseconds, faster than the generation itself.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Diffusion models generate images by iteratively denoising random noise, and their training relies on learning a score function that approximates the gradient of the data distribution's log-density. Training data attribution (TDA) aims to trace a generated output back to the specific training samples that influenced it, but traditional methods require expensive per-sample gradient computations or query-specific model optimization. Score discrepancy measures the difference between score functions, and Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) is a second-order approximation of the Fisher information matrix that makes curvature-based computations tractable for deep networks.

## [Persistent Calibration Under Evolving Model Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38797) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces the problem of persistent calibration, requiring confidence estimators to remain accurate as a model's knowledge evolves without recurring supervision. It evaluates this across checkpoints of open models using knowledge contrast sets, showing that inference-time and fine-tuning methods fall short compared to oracle methods trained on future checkpoints. As AI systems shift from static repositories to continually adapting agents, maintaining trustworthy confidence estimates is critical for AI safety and reliable deployment. This work highlights a gap in current calibration methods that could affect continual learning and model evaluation practices. The study defines calibration on knowledge contrast sets—subsets where one checkpoint answers correctly and another incorrectly—and finds that even methods well-calibrated on the full dataset fail on these sets. Multi-checkpoint training is shown to help, suggesting a path to identify robust confidence features.

A new arXiv preprint (2609.38802) introduces Tokenwise Residual Comparison (TRC), a diagnostic method that compares attention and MLP writes to the residual stream across generated tokens to localize anomalies tied to uncontrolled repetition, then selectively suppresses the offending coordinates at the identified layer. Experiments show TRC reduces loop rates by 57% on average and generalizes to LLMs and large reasoning models (LRMs). TRC works by comparing attention and multilayer perceptron writes to the residual stream across generated tokens, then selectively suppressing coordinates at the layer where repetition anomalies are identified; the analysis finds that repetition semantics emerge in shallow layers and propagate through the residual stream, disrupting normal representations.

Researchers propose StateTree, a data-driven reinforcement learning method that builds a tree-structured path-tracing auxiliary task from multi-session dialogues with verifiable ground truth. Trained on 10K-token contexts, StateTree-7B gains up to +23.60% on LongMemEval (128k), and StateTree-14B reaches 59.00% accuracy, surpassing QwenLong-L1-32B's 45.20%. Long-term dialogue reasoning is a core challenge for deploying LLMs as personalized assistants, where evidence is scattered across sessions and preferences change over time. StateTree shows that a small, verifiable auxiliary RL task can generalize from short 10K-token training to 128K-token inference without full-length RL costs, offering a cheaper path to long-context personalization. The task embeds key-value records across sessions into a binary tree; the model must traverse from root to leaf by retrieving records and comparing timestamps to resolve branches, then recover a hidden target question among distractor leaves. A compositional variant adds step-level reasoning fragments on edges, and curriculum RL progressively increases tree depth; the method preserves short-context general reasoning.

A new arXiv preprint (2609.38819) hypothesizes and provides initial fMRI evidence that internal representations used by autoregressive video diffusion models to generate future frames align better with human visual cortex responses than representations of the observed video itself. The study compares an autoregressive (AR) video diffusion model with its non-AR base model, finding that future-generation representations align more strongly with higher-order visual cortex, while observed-video reconstruction aligns with lower-order visual cortex. It also implies that generative objectives, not just perceptual ones, could be key to explaining how the visual cortex works. The alignment difference is region-specific: observed-video reconstruction concentrates in lower-order visual cortex, whereas future-frame generation concentrates in higher-order visual cortex. A human behavioral experiment further showed that people prefer videos generated by amplifying the contributions of individual layers that align better with the visual cortex.

## [Online-ES Adapts Flow-Matching VLA Policies via Evolution Strategy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38855) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Online-ES, an online adaptation framework that applies Evolution Strategy (ES) to refine the action trajectory distribution of Flow Matching-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation. Rather than pruning the latent noise space, it perturbs sampled trajectories, evaluates their execution outcomes, and derives a self-supervised MSE objective that transfers the evolution direction from trajectory space into model parameter space. This offers a way to improve generative robot policies online without learning a value model or computing advantages, achieving policy improvement comparable to reinforcement fine-tuning. It could make VLA deployment more practical in real-world settings where reward modeling is costly and failure data is abundant. The authors mathematically prove that the proposed objective is an unbiased estimator of the optimal evolution direction, and they incorporate failure experiences as negative feedback to steer the policy away from previously explored failure regions. Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments validate the approach.

## [Audio Token Attention Predictable Before Language Model Runs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38878) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38878) shows that the all-layer attention an audio token will receive in a large audio language model (LALM) is linearly predictable from its encoder output before the language model runs, with a closed-form, label-free linear map achieving rank correlation ρ ≥ .69 on eleven of thirteen LALMs. Based on this, the authors propose Triage, a token pruning method that cuts audio tokens before the language model and then re-cuts at layer 2 using observed attention. This finding is significant because existing multimodal token pruning methods typically cut after the language model's first layers, which works for image tokens that draw little attention there but fails for audio tokens that draw much more attention and whose ranking is far from final. Triage's pre-LM pruning raises the audio that fits in Qwen2.5-Omni-3B's context window from 21.8 to about 62 minutes and lets one GPU serve 4x as many concurrent 5-minute streams, directly improving the efficiency of long-audio inference. Triage sets its compression without labels under two budgets that limit how far its output may deviate from the model's own full-audio output; at the conservative budget, word error rate and accuracy stay within .04 of full audio, while at the aggressive budget it beats every baseline in all twelve transcription cases. On multiple choice at 2.2–5x compression, it outperforms DART, the strongest baseline on average, by .043 in mean accuracy.

A new arXiv paper introduces OptTips, a knowledge base of 50 expert optimization modeling techniques across eight families, and OptDachshund, a multi-agent framework that builds the EfficientOpt benchmark of 561 expert-reviewed tasks with paired conventional and expert reference implementations. Evaluating 11 representative LLMs, the authors find that on correctly solved tasks, most generated programs take longer to solve than their expert counterparts, with 57% of correct programs in the comparable reference-size subset having longer recorded solver times despite fewer variables and linear constraints. The study notes that different modeling techniques can reach the same optimal value at similar recorded cost, and that faster solving may not reduce total execution time if the generated code spends longer preparing data and building the model. ## [Stochastic Hybrid Systems Approximated by Continuous Latent SDEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38893) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.38893) proves that a stochastic hybrid system (SHS) can be approximated by a continuous stochastic differential equation (SDE) in a higher-dimensional latent space. The key trick is encoding the reset kernel's branches as auxiliary variables, turning stochastic resets into deterministic ones so the resulting manifold can be glued and embedded, eliminating explicit reset terms from the hybrid Fokker-Planck (HFP) equation. This offers a new theoretical bridge between hybrid and purely continuous stochastic models, potentially simplifying the modeling, simulation, and control of systems that switch between continuous dynamics and discrete jumps. It is directly relevant to researchers in dynamical systems, robotics, and machine learning who currently rely on mode labeling, trajectory segmentation, or event-based simulation. The construction uses an embedding theorem to map the glued manifold into a higher-dimensional Euclidean space, and the authors design a loss that matches evolving state distributions so a single latent SDE can recover the SHS probability evolution without mode labeling, trajectory segmentation, or event-based simulation. As a preprint, the result is theoretical and has not yet been peer-reviewed or validated on large-scale benchmarks.

**Background**: A stochastic hybrid system combines continuous stochastic dynamics, governed by an SDE, with discrete jumps triggered when the state hits a guard surface; the jump behavior is described by a Markov reset kernel. Its probability density evolves according to a hybrid Fokker-Planck equation, which contains both a partial differential term for the continuous flow and an integral term for the resets. The Fokker-Planck equation is the standard partial differential equation describing how a probability density function evolves under drift and diffusion.

## [Unmerge: Machine Unlearning as Inverse Task Arithmetic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38895) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper recasts approximate machine unlearning as the inverse of task arithmetic: instead of adding a task vector, it subtracts a low-rank forget component τ_F from a merged task vector τ_m to recover the retain task vector τ_R without retraining. The resulting algorithm, Unmerge, improves Tug-of-War by up to ~24% over a comparable-runtime baseline and up to ~18% over stronger baselines that run about 5x slower, on class-level unlearning with ResNet-50 on CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet. Machine unlearning is increasingly important for privacy compliance, copyright removal, and correcting harmful or stale knowledge in deployed models, where full retraining is often prohibitively expensive. By framing unlearning as inverse task arithmetic with a low-rank forget basis, Unmerge offers an interpretable, data-independent alternative to gradient-based methods that require costly hyperparameter search and struggle when forget and retain knowledge are entangled. The method factorizes τ_F in a low-rank forget basis, since forget activations at every layer lie in a subspace spanned by a handful of dominant directions, and it optimizes three goals—matching the merged vector inside the forget span, suppressing leakage into the retain span, and bounding correction size—that provably bound forget leakage and retain damage in activation space. It keeps membership-inference exposure at retraining level, shrinks the feature-distribution gap to the retrained model, and also applies to ViT-S/16 and scales to Llama-3.2-3B.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Machine unlearning refers to removing the influence of specific training data—such as private, copyrighted, or harmful content—from a trained model without rebuilding it from scratch. Task arithmetic is a model-editing technique in which a task vector is computed by subtracting pre-trained weights from fine-tuned weights, and these vectors can be added or negated to steer model behavior. Low-rank factorization approximates a large matrix using smaller rank-limited components, which is commonly used for compression and here captures the concentrated structure of the forget signal.

A new arXiv preprint (2609.38909) proposes PACT, a contrastive unlearning method that removes deceptive behaviors from LLMs by contrasting the same question under deception-triggering and neutral contexts, rather than forgetting factual knowledge. PACT instead trains toward pressure-aware counterfactual targets that register the pressure and resist it; it scores 0.94 and 0.86 on a tug-of-war metric of removal versus retention, versus at most 0.77 and 0.60 for baselines, though removed deception remains shallow under relearning.
