A new arXiv preprint (2609.38955) introduces Loop-Free Inverse Reinforcement Learning (LFIRL), which eliminates the bi-level reward-policy optimization loop in IRL by leveraging diffusion policies. LFIRL recovers the optimal soft Q function via action-gradient matching, calibrates soft values with a state-dependent offset, and extracts rewards through Bellman consistency, achieving 2-3x speedup over the fastest baselines on Maze, Franka Kitchen, Adroit Hand Pen, and Push-T benchmarks. Existing IRL methods rely on bi-level optimization that alternates between reward learning and policy optimization, causing high computational cost and training instability. The method proceeds in three stages: recovering the soft Q function via action-gradient matching with a Gumbel-regression-inspired LogSumExp value estimate, calibrating soft values with a state-dependent offset, and extracting rewards by enforcing Bellman consistency. It is a fully offline algorithm that matches or surpasses state-of-the-art reward recovery quality while being simple to implement.

Diffusion policies are a recent class of expressive generative models used as policies in reinforcement learning, and soft Q-learning provides a framework where the optimal policy is tied to a soft value function. LFIRL combines these ideas to recover rewards without ever running policy optimization.

On the JHTDB256 benchmark (256³), it achieves 53% lower NMSE than the strongest baseline and 79% lower training memory than the most memory-efficient baseline, and it reduces one-step NMSE by 65.8% for urban wind prediction on a 500×150×500 grid in Montreal. Neither model operates on the full-resolution field: the Child is pretrained alone and then attached to the Parent's coarse prediction via zero-initialized connections, which preserve the pretrained behavior at the start of joint training. The Parent can also be swapped for one trained on additional coarse fields to improve accuracy without retraining the Child, at only a small storage cost.

## [French and Regional Languages Pay a Token Tax in 2026 LLM Tokenizers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39001) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper measures token premiums across seven 2026-era tokenizers (OpenAI o200k, Llama 3, Qwen3, DeepSeek V3/V4, Gemma 3, Mistral Tekken, and Claude generation-5) on NTREX-128 and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, finding French needs 31%–58% more tokens than English and French regional languages 1.6–3.3x more. The findings are relevant to multilingual NLP researchers, cost modelers, and anyone deploying agents in non-English languages. The study covers seven tokenizers and finds Simplified Chinese ranges from 5% fewer to 40% more tokens than English and is cheaper than French on six of seven tokenizers; the French-optimized prototype is worse on other languages and does not beat CroissantLLM at comparable vocabulary size, and the paper stresses these are segmentation results only with no demonstrated effect on model quality or task cost.

Forward calculation on the quality assurance CT reduced high-dose CTV D98% to 88.3% and 85.5%, but after online reoptimization D98% recovered to 98.3 ± 0.3% and 98.2 ± 0.3%, versus 98.5 ± 0.4% at baseline, with spinal cord and brainstem doses remaining below tolerance.

A new arXiv paper evaluates 13 validators in a deployed generative agent against 550 runtime and 350 static builds, finding that only two checks survive correction for multiple comparisons, two are nominal only, and nine are indistinguishable from zero. This finding has direct implications for deployment pipelines that rely on validator checks as hard gates, showing that an inventory of checks is not evidence about a gate's actual effectiveness. The study uses Newcombe intervals and Fisher exact tests, and replicates its execution-bias finding across four runs covering 1,867 builds and ten distinct runtime checks, with every skip carrying the same unsafe-to-probe reason. For one check with construct-specific labels, a detector built for blank output fires on 0 of 90 human-labelled blank builds (95% upper bound on sensitivity 3.3%), and the global frame statistic it approximates separates classes only weakly (AUC 0.59), indicating the gap is not a threshold-tuning problem.

The performance asymmetry across VAD dimensions closely mirrors the annotator agreement hierarchy in IEMOCAP's own annotations.

## [HO-FL: Hybrid-Order Federated Learning for Memory-Constrained Edge Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39074) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers from HKU-WILL-Lab introduced HO-FL, a hybrid-order federated learning framework that trains a model's bottom segment with zeroth-order (ZO) optimization and its top segment with first-order (FO) optimization, letting each device choose its order boundary based on its memory budget. Their convergence analysis reveals a new bias-variance trade-off in client sampling: clients with larger FO-trained segments give more accurate updates, but favoring them underrepresents other clients' data. This work addresses a core dilemma in federated learning on edge devices, where FO optimization (backpropagation) demands substantial memory while ZO optimization converges much more slowly. By retaining much of full-FO performance at substantially lower client memory, HO-FL could make federated training practical on a wider range of heterogeneous, memory-constrained devices. The paper connects the sampling trade-off to the bias and variance of actual multi-step local updates, yielding a sampling optimization problem and a practical dimension-aware approximation with direct model averaging. Experiments on language tasks evaluate task performance, client memory, and sampling under data heterogeneity, and the code is available at https://github.com/HKU-WILL-Lab/HO-FL.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Federated learning (FL) lets many edge devices collaboratively train a shared global model without sharing raw private data. First-order optimization, i.e., backpropagation, computes gradients accurately but must store intermediate activations, which is costly on memory-limited devices; zeroth-order optimization estimates gradients from function evaluations alone, avoiding that memory but converging much more slowly. HO-FL sits between these extremes by splitting the model into ZO-trained and FO-trained segments, and client sampling—choosing which devices participate in each round—is a long-studied issue in FL because biased sampling can skew the global model.

## [APST transformer enables frozen-weight cross-session intracortical motor decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39080) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present APST, an Association Profile-conditioned Set-Temporal transformer that adapts to new recording sessions with all network weights frozen. Using only a few labeled calibration trials, it computes a four-dimensional association profile per unit in closed form, and reaches velocity R² of 0.78 and 0.81 on held-out DANDI688 sessions from two monkeys, versus 0.40 and 0.58 for a neural-activity-only variant. APST uses a set-attention encoder that accepts any number and order of units, followed by a causal transformer for streaming decoding, and it matches or exceeds an RNN fine-tuned on the same calibration trials. ## [Paper Diagnoses 'Co-Cheating' in Self-Evolving Search Agents, Proposes CrossFit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39102) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.39102) identifies a failure mode called 'co-cheating' in self-evolving search agents, where the proposer that generates questions and the solver that answers them increasingly agree on shared errors, so internal reward rises without external correctness improving. The authors propose multi-sample verification (MSV) as a partial fix and CrossFit as the main method, which partitions source documents into groups A and B and scores questions with an auxiliary solver trained only on the other group. Self-evolving agents that build their own training curricula are a fast-growing paradigm for improving LLM search and reasoning without human-labeled data, so a failure mode that inflates internal reward while degrading real correctness threatens the reliability of the whole approach. The paper's diagnosis and CrossFit mitigation offer a concrete path to keep such self-improvement loops honest, which matters for AI safety and for anyone deploying self-improving search agents. MSV queries the same model three times with the source and three times without it to decide task admission and replace unreliable pseudo-labels, but it only reduces false-agreement mass from 6.1% to 5.7% (Qwen3.5-4B) and from 8.8% to 7.2% (Qwen3.5-9B) while costing six extra labeler generations per candidate. CrossFit cuts false agreement to 3.0% and 3.7%, and replaying identical proposals with source-excluded feedback drops it further to 0.4% and 0.1%; across seven downstream search benchmarks CrossFit improves average performance by 8.8 and 8.4 points over standard coupled self-evolution and by 8.7 and 7.8 points over Search-R1 at 4B and 9B.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Self-evolving search agents typically use a self-play loop in which a 'proposer' generates questions from source documents and a 'solver' answers them, with the solver's performance providing the reward signal that trains both components. Because no external ground-truth labels are used, the system relies on pseudo-labels, and if proposer and solver share the same model biases they can reinforce each other's mistakes — a form of reward hacking related to Goodhart's law. CrossFit borrows the idea of cross-fitting from statistics: by scoring questions with a solver that never saw the source document they came from, it prevents the feedback solver from simply reproducing the same-source pseudo-label.

## [T-Router: Thalamic Routing for Parameter-Efficient Reasoning RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39109) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint introduces the Thalamic Router (T-Router), a parameter-efficient reinforcement learning method that learns context-dependent routing to reuse completed computations. On an 8.95B-parameter backbone, T-Router trains only 41.73M parameters (0.466% of the backbone) and reaches 83.64 ± 1.16 MathAvg after GSM8K RL, versus 73.79 ± 1.83 for full-parameter GRPO, while also beating LoRA's 77.28 ± 1.95 and lifting mean AIME accuracy from 48.33 to 60.56. The result suggests that concentrating adaptation on the reuse of prior computations can outperform full-parameter RL fine-tuning at a tiny fraction of the trainable budget, which could make reasoning-oriented RL far cheaper for large models. If it generalizes, it may shift parameter-efficient fine-tuning practice away from simple low-rank adapters toward learned routing interfaces. T-Router keeps a compressed, addressable bank of block changes and uses a depth-recurrent controller to select which earlier contributions a receiving layer reuses and at what relative scale, with correctness rewards training only the interface while backbone parameters and layer order stay frozen. Capacity-controlled comparisons favor addressable block changes and recurrent context, and separate search training extends the interface to tool-mediated reasoning.

**Background**: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model by training only a small set of extra or selected parameters, and LoRA is the most common example. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), proposed by DeepSeek, is a reinforcement learning algorithm for LLMs that uses group-based normalization to compute relative policy advantages instead of a value critic. T-Router borrows its name from the thalamus, the brain region that routes and gates information between cortical areas, and applies that idea as a learned routing mechanism over a frozen backbone.

## [Blackout vs. Freeze: How VLA Robots Fail Under Camera Faults](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39145) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.39145) empirically analyzes how the π0.5 and GR00T vision-language-action models behave physically when camera inputs suffer blackouts or freezing. It finds that the two fault types produce distinct failure modes even when task-success rates are similarly low: freezing leads to more extreme joint behavior, while blackout after gripper closure causes more object drops, especially without proprioception. As VLA models move toward real-world deployment in safety-critical robotics, understanding how they fail physically under unreliable perception is essential for risk assessment and certification. The findings suggest that safety evaluations based only on task-success rates can miss hazardous motion patterns that matter for human-robot coexistence. Selective intervention studies show that proprioception (the robot's current state) partially compensates for removed robot depictions and reduces non-target contact, but cannot restore task success when wrist-view object information is removed, even with the remaining scene view. Two mitigations—camera-blackout training and training-free replacement of faulty visual embeddings—improve success in selected conditions but can increase unintended contact or disturbance to surrounding objects, and real-robot trials show successful execution can still involve unintended physical interactions.

## [DAGent: Evaluate-then-Grow Planning for Deep Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39154) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DAGent introduces an Evaluate-then-Grow incremental planning framework for DAG-based multi-agent deep research agents, replacing the brittle Plan-then-Patch strategy with a graph that grows one batch at a time based on confidence and uncertainty signals from completed nodes. It also proposes DAGRPO, a GRPO adaptation that injects topology-conditioned credit on Executor rollouts and structural compliance regularization on Orchestrator plans. This addresses a real limitation of existing DAG-based agents, which commit to a full task-level plan before execution and only repair the graph after failures, wasting computation and making decisions most strongly when evidence is weakest. The reported gains across BrowseComp-Plus, GAIA, and xbench-DeepSearch suggest a more efficient and accurate planning paradigm for deep research agents. DAGent surpasses the strongest open-source baseline by 5.3 / 5.8 / 2.0 points at the Qwen3-235B-A22B scale across the three benchmarks, with the lead replicating across four open-source backbones and extending to GPT-5 at 327K context; at the Qwen3-8B scale, DAGRPO improves over a same-budget outcome-only GRPO baseline by 3.0 average Pass@1 points. A hierarchical context layer propagates compact QueryDocs by default while preserving full execution traces for on-demand recall.

**Background**: Deep research tasks require agents to navigate large knowledge spaces, synthesize evidence across many sources, and adapt plans as findings emerge. FDCU uses an element-wise dual-masking rule: it preserves general knowledge manifolds via Fisher Information and prohibits abnormal activation of spurious suppressors via the Principle of Minimal Functional Intervention (PMFI). Experiments show state-of-the-art robustness against retraining attacks while maintaining near-lossless general utility.

## [EngramBench: A Capability-Grounded Benchmark for Skill-Evolution Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39284) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced EngramBench, a new benchmark governed by the axiom of "capability overlap without solution overlap," comprising 30 diverse learning tasks and 13 unseen transfer tasks designed to disentangle genuine skill abstraction from rote solution leakage in autonomous software engineering agents. Evaluation across 48 multi-hour execution trajectories, validated by human experts, shows that static skill banks reduce overall coding time by over 55% but cannot bypass the "last mile" of exact code implementation. This work addresses a critical identifiability problem in evaluating skill evolution: existing benchmarks structurally confound genuine capability abstraction with rote solution leakage from training data, inflating apparent agent competence. By shifting evaluation from trivial pattern matching to verifiable cross-domain capability transfer, EngramBench offers a more rigorous standard for measuring whether autonomous coding agents truly learn reusable skills. The benchmark uses LLM-simulated users to drive interactive, multi-hour development cycles, and its findings distinguish two roles of procedural memory: static skill banks act as an "execution compass" that avoids token-heavy trial-and-error, yet the base model's inherent reasoning limits still bottleneck exact code implementation. As an arXiv preprint, it has not yet undergone peer review or visible community discussion.

## [Rollout Scale and Selection Rules Make Automatic Harness Evolution Work for Robot Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39304) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.39304) shows that the hand-written harness — prompts, tools, and control rules — of a coding agent acting as a visual-interface robot policy can be improved automatically by a second coding agent, the optimizer agent. Two findings stand out: growing the training set from 5 to 100 rollouts per round raises held-out success from 47% to 67%, and adding a simple Champion-Challenger selection rule lifts held-out success from 51% to 67% over 30 rounds, whereas unconditional acceptance causes performance to drift downward within ten rounds. This work suggests that agent harnesses, currently hand-crafted and brittle, can be evolved automatically, which could reduce engineering effort and improve reliability for robot agents that operate through screenshots and virtual tools. The empirical link between rollout batch size and generalization also gives practitioners a concrete, measurable lever for designing agent-optimization loops. A single rollout is a noisy binary outcome, so promoting revisions on small batches risks rewarding luck: small training sets reached 70% on training tasks but only 54% held-out, while larger batches raised the signal-to-noise ratio of every promotion decision. The safeguard used is Champion-Challenger selection, which promotes a revision only if it strictly beats the incumbent on the same fixed evaluation set.

## [ActionGuard Authorizes Tool Calls to Block Poisoned Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39450) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.39450) introduces ActionGuard, a security mechanism that intercepts skill-influenced Tool Calls at OpenClaw's before-tool-call stage and enforces a Reviewer's ALLOW or DENY decision under a fail-closed policy. Evaluated on 139 contextual and 180 obvious injections against Dynamic Guardian and SkillGuard, ActionGuard reduced Attack Success Rate by 35.54–46.11% versus existing safeguards and by 70.44% versus no safeguard, while maintaining high benign-task completion. LLM agents increasingly rely on third-party skills that form a new supply-chain attack surface, so a defense that authorizes actions at the execution boundary addresses a top-ranked risk (prompt injection) for agentic systems. This matters to agent platform developers, skill marketplace operators, and security teams who need practical safeguards without sacrificing task completion. ActionGuard separates the target agent's action-generation context from the safeguard's authorization context: the agent may still plan with the original skill, but the Reviewer never sees the potentially poisoned raw skill text, instead judging each action against the trusted user request, a balanced skill profile, current and recent Tool Calls, and local script contents. The evaluation used three open-source and two commercial Reviewer models, repeating each condition three times and measuring Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Task Success Rate (TSR).

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: LLM-based agents extend their abilities through third-party skills that bundle task-specific instructions, scripts, and tool-use procedures; tool calling is the mechanism by which a model emits a structured signal to invoke an external function such as a search, database query, or code execution. Because skills are loaded as trusted guidance, a malicious instruction hidden inside an otherwise benign skill can make a normal user request trigger dangerous Tool Calls like data exfiltration, file deletion, or unauthorized code execution — a form of indirect prompt injection that OWASP ranks as the top LLM vulnerability. OpenClaw is an agent runtime that exposes plugin hooks such as before_tool_call, allowing a plugin to observe or block tool calls before they execute.

## [CAMOS: Coupled Oscillatory State-Space Model for Missing Clinical Modalities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39484) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers posted an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2609.39484) introducing CAMOS, a coupled oscillatory state-space model in which each modality is represented by a bank of second-order oscillators coupled through a matrix that sits inside the differential equation and is gated by modality availability. The paper also proves that any linear state-space layer whose transition operator ignores the availability pattern cannot represent interactions between modalities being jointly present or jointly absent, and it reports that CAMOS beats uncoupled oscillatory SSMs and clinical fusion models on ADNI staging, landmark prediction and forecasting, while avoiding majority-class collapse in zero-shot transfer to OASIS-3. Clinical cohorts such as ADNI routinely have missing modalities — PET and CSF assays are absent from roughly half of all visits — so a model that explicitly encodes which measurements were taken could substantially improve robustness and fairness of longitudinal clinical prediction. The theoretical result also matters beyond healthcare, because it shows that the common practice of masking missing inputs in linear state-space models is not merely an engineering inconvenience but a provable representational limitation. To keep the coupled system stable, the authors introduce a per-channel Gershgorin budget that makes the effective stiffness positive definite uniformly over all 2^M availability patterns and all time gaps, an energy argument that charges amplification to availability transitions rather than sequence length, and a channel factorization that preserves exact associative parallel scans. Evaluation is limited to ADNI and OASIS-3, and the work is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: State-space models (SSMs) are a family of sequence models, popularized by S4 and Mamba, that describe a latent state evolving over time through a transition operator and are especially efficient for long or irregularly sampled sequences. In multimodal clinical data, each modality (e.g., imaging, fluid biomarkers, cognitive scores) is measured at different, irregular times, and standard practice is to mask the missing inputs while leaving the transition operator unchanged. Coupled oscillator models, inspired by systems like the Kuramoto model, instead let multiple oscillatory units interact, which is the mechanism CAMOS adapts to make the transition operator itself depend on which modalities are present.

## [PartiCam: Training-Free Particle Filtering for Camera-Controlled Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39504) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PartiCam introduces a training-free particle filtering method with a global-local refinement framework to improve camera trajectory control in video diffusion models. It builds on Sequential Monte-Carlo (SMC) guidance and adds a local refinement stage based on particle-filtered resampling, yielding better camera trajectory adherence, reduced drift, and improved visual quality without retraining the model. Camera-controlled video generation is a key capability for filmmaking, virtual production, and synthetic data creation, but existing sampling-based guidance often produces unstable trajectories. PartiCam's training-free approach is backbone-agnostic and can generate camera-controlled video data to train future camera-conditioned diffusion models, potentially lowering the cost of building such systems. The method addresses two failure modes of existing sampling-based guidance: exploring too broadly and failing to respect the target camera motion, or collapsing early and losing visual diversity over time. It combines Sequential Monte-Carlo guidance with particle-filtered resampling for local refinement, and experiments show large improvements in trajectory adherence and drift reduction without model retraining.

**Background**: Video diffusion models generate videos by iteratively denoising random noise, extending image diffusion architectures to the temporal domain. Reward guidance steers a pretrained generative process toward a desired property at inference time, but can suffer from reward hacking or unstable trajectories. PartiCam applies these ideas to steer video diffusion models along a specified camera path without any fine-tuning.

## [NDDL: Learning Normal Diffusion Dynamics for T2I Backdoor Defense](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39548) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes NDDL (Normal Diffusion Dynamics Learning), a backdoor defense framework for text-to-image diffusion models that learns the normal transition dynamics of benign diffusion trajectories and flags deviations caused by backdoor attacks. It constructs compact multi-space trajectory representations from cross-attention, latent, and noise spaces, trains a timestep-conditioned dynamics model to predict diffusion evolution, and uses observed-versus-predicted transition deviations to detect backdoors and localize triggers via low-semantic word substitution. Backdoor attacks threaten the secure deployment of text-to-image diffusion models, and existing defenses that rely on specific abnormal patterns in internal representations may not generalize to increasingly diverse attack mechanisms. By shifting to a transition-dynamics perspective that uses only benign samples, NDDL offers a more generalizable detection angle that could strengthen AI security for generative image systems. NDDL requires only benign samples for training and needs no prior knowledge of the embedded backdoor, enabling trigger localization through substitution with low-semantic words. The paper reports extensive experiments across diverse backdoor attacks demonstrating effectiveness and generalizability, though it remains an arXiv preprint without peer review.

Backdoor attacks embed hidden triggers into such models so that specific inputs cause malicious or unintended outputs, and defenses typically try to detect these anomalies. Prior work such as T2IShield detects backdoors via an "Assimilation Phenomenon" in cross-attention maps, while NDDL instead models the normal timestep-dependent evolution of diffusion trajectories as a baseline for anomaly detection.

## [Speculative Safety Honeypot: Proactive Defense Against Multi-turn Agent Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39549) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes the Speculative Safety Honeypot (SSH) framework, which uses a multi-agent simulation system of small LLMs to predict a target agent's future actions and asynchronously build a trajectory tree, then verifies and prunes it with the agent's real actions. This plug-and-play component gives existing detectors decision redundancy beyond the current interaction slice, improving warning lead-time against multi-turn attacks. Multi-turn attacks that split malicious intent across turns can evade retrospective detectors, so a proactive, trajectory-level defense could significantly harden LLM agent deployments in complex environments. If validated, SSH could shift agent security from single-point filtering toward anticipatory risk assessment. SSH is inspired by speculative decoding: small LLMs speculate future behaviors and build a trajectory tree, while the target agent's real actions calibrate and prune the tree to reduce false positives. Risk is judged by the evolution of the entire trajectory tree rather than a single point in time, reducing reliance on the absolute precision of individual detection components.

**Background**: Speculative decoding is an inference-time optimization in which a smaller draft model proposes multiple candidate tokens and a larger target model verifies them in parallel, preserving output quality while speeding up generation. Multi-turn attacks, by contrast, deliver carefully crafted prompts across several conversation turns to gradually manipulate an LLM into harmful behavior, exploiting stateless guardrails. SSH adapts the speculate-and-verify idea from token generation to agent action trajectories, using a tree of possible futures as the unit of security analysis.

## [GroundAnything: 4B Diffusion Model Achieves Fast Parallel Visual Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39600) ⭐️ 7.0/10

GroundAnything is a 4B-parameter diffusion-based grounding foundation model that replaces autoregressive sequential decoding with blockwise denoising to enable fast parallel spatial prediction. Its autoregressive variant, GroundAnything-VLM, reaches 72.42% across 30 grounding benchmarks, and an entropy-guided decoding mode averages 61.75% versus 53.32% for the fast MTP-based LocateAnything model. The work challenges the assumption that visual grounding must be generated left-to-right, showing that bidirectional diffusion can deliver both precision and speed for latency-sensitive applications like robotics and real-time multimodal assistants. It also demonstrates that autoregressive models can be converted to diffusion models without retraining from scratch, which could lower the cost of building fast grounding systems. Training combines grounding pretraining from public datasets and dedicated data engines, direct AR-to-diffusion conversion with joint AR and diffusion objectives, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO-based reinforcement post-training. An optional self-speculative decoding mode achieves a 4.51x speedup over the autoregressive counterpart with only a 0.74 percentage-point drop in COCO F1mIoU.

The authors generalize this to a one-parameter family with PPO (alpha=0) and the full correction (alpha=1) as endpoints, and show on hard credit-assignment scheduling tasks that a short corrected warmup with aggressive early sample reuse learns faster than PPO (+0.02 to +0.09 learning-curve AUC). This matters because aggressive off-policy reuse of a batch is normally blocked by the bias that grows with policy divergence, forcing trust regions or clipping; an exact correction could let practitioners reuse data far off-policy and improve sample efficiency in RL for LLMs, where autoregressive generation is history-injective. The exact correction pays an importance-sampling variance that grows with the horizon, which is why the authors introduce the alpha knob; a gradient-level analysis of the unclipped surrogate identifies two channels the correction acts through and three conditions under which it carries signal, and the paper warns that a correction held throughout, or applied where clipping already contains the reuse bias, is null to harmful.

## [SIM Diagnostic Predicts When Masking Hurts Compressed CLIP Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39704) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces the Spurious Inversion Metric (SIM), a label-free, pre-deployment diagnostic that predicts whether masking-based token pruning will improve or degrade worst-group robustness in compressed CLIP models. Across 8 spurious-correlation benchmarks and 6 CLIP architectures, the sign of SIM predicts the effect with statistical significance (binomial p=0.035), and gating deployment by SIM's sign matches or exceeds a strong pruning baseline on 7 of 8 datasets. Masking-based token pruning is widely used to cut the cost of deploying CLIP-like vision-language models, but its effect on worst-group robustness is highly unstable, improving accuracy by up to 82.5% relative on some datasets and degrading it by up to 100% on others. A cheap, label-free pre-deployment check lets practitioners decide whether to enable masking before committing to a deployment, avoiding silent failures on minority subgroups. The instability is traced to 'spurious inversion': when the spurious attribute is background-separable, background patches receive higher CLIP text-similarity than the true object, inverting the assumption that text- and attention-guided pruning methods rely on. Naive masking also causes the largest average-accuracy loss of any evaluated method, and its per-image segmentation step is a runtime bottleneck; the authors design a batched, synchronization-free GPU segmentation routine that cuts this overhead from 3.5x to 1.75x baseline.

## [Probabilistic Adversarial Training via a KL-Based Robustness Bound](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39798) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.39798) introduces probabilistic adversarial training, proving that KL(p_dis || p_vic) − log Z_vic is a lower bound on probabilistic robustness (PR). Maximizing this tractable surrogate recovers a scaled form of adversarial training, and experiments show it consistently improves PR, with the induced scaling factor even boosting non-probabilistic adversarial training methods. Adversarial training is one of the few defenses that empirically works against adversarial examples, yet it has long lacked a principled theoretical explanation. By deriving a KL-based lower bound on probabilistic robustness, this work offers a probabilistic interpretation of why adversarial training helps and a principled route to designing more robust models. The framework models adversarial examples as arising from the overlap between a distance-based distribution p_dis and a victim-classifier-induced distribution p_vic, and the bound involves the normalizing constant Z_vic of p_vic. Because probabilistic robustness is generally intractable to compute directly, the KL-based lower bound serves as a tractable surrogate objective, and ablation studies isolate the effect of the induced scaling factor.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Adversarial examples are inputs with small, intentional perturbations that cause a machine learning model to make a wrong prediction, and they expose surprising vulnerabilities in modern models. Adversarial training, which incorporates such examples into training, is among the most effective defenses, but it remains unclear why adversarial examples exist and how adversarial training improves robustness. KL divergence, a measure of how one probability distribution differs from another, is widely used in machine learning and information theory and here provides the mathematical bridge between distribution separation and robustness.

## [Stress-Testing LLM Lie Detectors: Role-Play Failures and Spurious Correlations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39807) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.39807) introduces a dataset of 8,916 human-reviewed, on-policy responses from three LLMs adopting anti-factual personas, and evaluates eight existing lie-detection probes on it. Many probes fail under this setting, especially when correct and incorrect answers are evaluated under the same persona prompt, and three novel confounder datasets show that probes often track concepts spuriously correlated with truth, such as instruction compliance or response likelihood. This work shows that current lie-detection probes for LLMs are far from reliable, which directly undermines interpretability-based deception detection and AI safety monitoring. It also argues that training data must decorrelate truth from confounding concepts, a finding that affects how the community builds and validates truthfulness evaluations. The authors propose a simple linear probe that achieves the strongest overall performance on both the persona and confounder stress tests, though the paper's core message is that existing probes are unreliable rather than that the problem is solved. The confounder datasets are constructed so that truth is anti-correlated with a potential confounding concept, isolating spurious reliance on instruction compliance and response likelihood.

Spurious correlations arise when a probe latches onto a feature that happens to correlate with truth in training data but is not causally related to honesty.

## [FailBank Turns Runtime Safety Feedback into Lasting VLA Policy Gains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39820) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce FailBank, a four-stage self-evolving framework that converts runtime safety corrections into persistent policy improvement for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. On the VLA-Arena benchmark, it raises task success rate by 8.5 and 6.9 percentage points across two VLA backbones while cutting policy-induced cumulative cost by 35.6% and 23.8%, and it beats runtime shielding by 25.4 and 9.5 percentage points in success rate. Runtime shields can veto unsafe actions but leave the underlying policy unchanged, so repeated corrections can stall task progress; FailBank shows that runtime feedback can instead serve as persistent policy supervision. This matters for robotics and embodied AI, where balancing task success with avoiding unintended contact is a core deployment challenge. The framework uses a fixed CBF-based safety module as an observe-only teacher that generates counterfactual corrections while the policy stays in control, then applies outcome-aware admission to turn useful proposals into corrective targets and keeps successful uncorrected actions as quiet anchors for guarded LoRA updates. Evaluation covers two difficulty levels and two VLA backbones on VLA-Arena, though the abstract is truncated and no community discussion is available.

Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) provide a rigorous mathematical framework for enforcing safety by keeping system states inside predefined safe sets, and are commonly used as runtime shields. ## [Synthetic Pre-pretraining Scales to 7B but Lacks Grammatical Prior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39827) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A comprehensive study spanning five pre-pretraining (PPT) tasks, four pre-training (PT) data mixtures, four model scales (500M to 7B parameters), and PT budgets up to 100B tokens shows that PPT's token-efficiency gains persist at scale, saving at least 21B PT tokens at the 3B scale. However, contrary to prior work, the study finds no consistent evidence that these gains stem from a grammatical prior; instead, gains arise from PPT tasks that improve long-range retrieval. This work challenges a widely held explanation for why synthetic pre-pretraining works, redirecting future PPT task design toward long-range retrieval rather than natural language grammar. It provides the LLM training community with large-scale empirical evidence that PPT remains a low-cost, robust addition to pre-training even under realistic data mixtures including code and math. The study tested PPT across four parameter scales (500M to 7B) and PT budgets up to 100B tokens, finding that gains are robust to how PT data mixtures are composed and diminish only when web text is absent. Downstream performance did not consistently align with grammatical acceptability across model sizes, undermining the grammatical-prior hypothesis.

## [Paper Exposes Role-Capability Leakage in Role-Prompted LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39846) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.39846) introduces the concept of role-capability leakage (RCL), where role-prompted reasoning models produce stylistically convincing in-role text while still solving problems far above their assigned role. The authors present RoleCapBench, a curriculum-grounded benchmark spanning six educational roles and four assessment levels from elementary school to A-level, and evaluate three open-weight reasoning models, finding strong role-voice scores of 1.218–1.389 alongside above-role accuracy of 0.811–0.898. This finding matters for AI safety and alignment because it shows that role prompting alone does not actually constrain a model's underlying capabilities, which could mislead users who assume a role-limited assistant is genuinely limited. It also has practical implications for prompt engineering, evaluation, and any deployment where models are expected to stay within a defined persona or competence boundary. The leakage persists even under prompts that explicitly instruct the model to match the role's capability level, and the authors propose Injection, an inference-time intervention combining role-specific capability guidelines with a guiding prefilled response prefix. Injection reduces above-role accuracy by up to 0.562 while preserving in-role accuracy with a marginal drop of less than 0.058 across most models; all artifacts will be released upon acceptance.

## [Algorithmic Recourse Under Competition Challenges Fixed-Threshold Assumption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39877) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.39877) introduces a framework called "recourse under competition" that challenges the standard assumption that the decision rule remains fixed during recourse implementation. It jointly optimizes which rejected individuals receive recommendations and what score targets they should aim for, using an algorithm based on the Implicit Function Theorem, and shows empirically that personalized score targets achieve higher validity at higher cost while common score targets offer better cost-validity trade-offs at lower to medium validity levels. This work is significant because most algorithmic recourse methods assume a static decision threshold, which breaks down when many individuals act on advice simultaneously and compete for limited resources such as loan approvals or job offers. It could affect real-world applications in lending, hiring, and admissions, where recourse recommendations may become invalid once enough people follow them, and it pushes the fairness and ML communities to account for strategic, equilibrium effects. The proposed algorithm leverages the Implicit Function Theorem to handle the threshold shift that occurs when widespread recourse changes the acceptance cutoff even though the underlying scoring model is unchanged. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets reveal a trade-off: personalized score targets yield higher post-shift validity but at greater cost, whereas common score targets generally provide favorable cost-validity trade-offs for lower to medium validity values.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Algorithmic recourse gives people who receive unfavorable decisions from machine learning models—such as loan denials—actionable suggestions for the minimum-cost changes needed to get a desired outcome. Traditionally, recourse computation assumes the model's decision rule stays fixed while people implement the suggested changes. However, in competitive settings where individuals vie for limited resources, if many people improve their scores, the acceptance threshold can rise, making the original advice insufficient. This paper models that competition explicitly and seeks recommendations that remain valid after the threshold shifts.

## [Goal Representation Quality Barely Matters in Offline GCRL, State Encoding Is the Real Bottleneck](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39901) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.39901) constructs an exact temporal-distance goal representation in deterministic mazes and then systematically corrupts its geometric quality while keeping the downstream learner fixed. Across OGBench navigation tasks and two algorithms, large changes in goal-representation quality produce almost no change in performance, whereas applying the same interventions to the agent's current state more than doubles success. The authors further show that simple random Fourier positional encodings substantially improve performance on the hardest navigation tasks without map information or objective modifications. This finding challenges a common assumption in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning that better goal representations are the key to better policies, redirecting attention toward the state representation pathway. It could influence future research directions in offline GCRL and navigation, suggesting that effort spent on elaborate goal encodings may be better invested in improving how the agent perceives its current state. The study is limited to state-based offline navigation in deterministic mazes and OGBench tasks, so the conclusions may not transfer to pixel-based or stochastic environments. The proposed fix, random Fourier positional encodings, is simple and requires no map information or objective modifications, but the paper notes that code will be released soon, so full reproducibility is pending.

## [CoVisco: Codec-Native Vision Encoder with Native Token Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39924) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CoVisco introduces a codec-native vision encoder that performs native token compression, encoding long image and video inputs in a single forward pass without dense patch-to-patch interactions across all frames. Pretrained on 565M image-text pairs and 6.4M videos, it uses only 400 visual tokens in abstract-only inference for a four-segment, 64-frame setting while matching or exceeding OneVision-Encoder on several video-understanding benchmarks. Visual token counts grow with both temporal duration and spatial resolution, making long-video understanding expensive for both the vision encoder and the language model. By integrating compression directly into the encoder rather than applying it post-hoc, CoVisco addresses a fundamental scaling bottleneck and could influence future multimodal architectures for efficient long-video understanding. CoVisco combines codec-native input support with segmented attention, equipping each temporal segment with learnable abstract tokens while keeping fine-grained patch tokens available throughout the encoder; alternating intra-segment and abstract-communication layers preserve video-level context. A lightweight selector exposes either abstract tokens alone or abstract tokens augmented with a runtime-selected subset of patch tokens, and selected patch tokens further improve fine-grained video reasoning.

The framework trains both stages with LoRA adapters—a localization LoRA to improve selected windows and an answer LoRA to improve answers read from those windows—and can localize candidate temporal windows over pre-computed transcripts without decoding media frames, while routing the final answering pass over raw audio-visual streams to preserve non-speech evidence. Researchers propose HiSentinel, a hindsight-distillation framework that trains lightweight 0.6B and 1.7B sentinel models to decide, before execution, whether a coding agent's proposed action should be allowed, autonomously redirected, or paused for human help. The framework uses Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct as a privileged teacher that sees recorded execution outcomes as evidence, then distills this into a causal student that only receives the pre-action context and the proposed action. The sentinel must not only decide whether and when to intervene but also produce actionable feedback that helps the agent recover or obtain necessary human input, while keeping token consumption competitive.

## [Fenchel Tilting: Weighted Correction for Efficient Generative Model Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40030) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce Fenchel Tilt Flow Control (FTFC), a method that decouples utility optimization from generative-model fitting by first fitting an effective reward and density-ratio weights on pretrained samples, then freezing those weights to modify a diffusion or flow model in a single stage of importance-weighted denoising or flow matching. Across image and molecule generation benchmarks, FTFC improves over baselines on diverse preference functions while being up to 20× more efficient. This work addresses a key trade-off in reward alignment for generative models, where existing fine-tuning methods either restrict the family of supported preferences or sacrifice efficiency. By supporting general f-divergence penalties and avoiding differentiation through sampling trajectories, FTFC could make preference alignment more practical for diffusion and flow models in image and molecule design. FTFC establishes exact duality for concave utilities under suitable conditions and shows that weighted fitting reproduces the optimal target distribution for a given utility. The method supports general f-divergence penalties that determine how rewards are transformed into distribution-correction weights, and it enables adaptation beyond expected-reward maximization without complex optimization.

**Background**: Fenchel duality is a mathematical result in convex analysis that relates a primal optimization problem to a dual problem via convex conjugates, and it is widely used in optimization theory. An f-divergence is a family of functions that measures the difference between two probability distributions, including KL-divergence and total variation distance as special cases. Diffusion models and flow models are generative models that learn to transform noise into data through iterative denoising or flow matching, and fine-tuning them to satisfy preferences typically requires reward alignment techniques.

## [GGSD uses self-play to discover human-playable motor skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40137) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present Game-Guided Skill Discovery (GGSD), a framework that uses self-play in competitive games to discover a small set of discrete, interpretable motor skills that humans can directly control. After training, a human replaces the high-level policy and steers the agent through the same discrete skills, with skill transitions producing emergent combo behaviors across Ant, Franka-arm, and Unitree G1 environments. This work addresses a key challenge in embodied AI: making learned skills semantically distinct, interpretable, and expressive enough for humans to actually play with. It could improve human-agent interaction and game AI by letting people compose a handful of learned primitives to solve unseen tasks without additional training. GGSD uses a hierarchical agent that competes against its past selves, with a high-level policy selecting from a small discrete skill set and a skill-conditioned low-level policy learning the corresponding behaviors. Despite the small number of high-level actions, skill transitions give rise to emergent combo behaviors that expand expressivity beyond individual primitives, and humans can compose these skills to solve unseen tasks such as Maze and CubePush.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Unsupervised skill discovery in reinforcement learning aims to learn diverse, reusable behaviors without task-specific rewards, but existing methods often struggle to produce skills that are simultaneously distinct, interpretable, and expressive. Hierarchical reinforcement learning separates decision-making into a high-level policy that picks skills or subgoals and a low-level policy that executes them over many steps. Self-play, where agents train against historical versions of themselves, has driven breakthroughs in competitive games such as Go and poker, and GGSD combines these ideas to ground skill discovery in gameplay.

## [PrefPI steers robot policies into out-of-distribution behaviors via preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40165) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PrefPI (Preference-Guided Policy Iteration) is an iterative framework that steers pretrained generative robot policies toward behaviors rarely or never seen under the initial policy, using only relative preferences over self-generated trajectories. On real hardware it raised object transport height from 10.7 cm to 19.8 cm using just 150 preference-labeled trajectories, and it worked across diffusion policies and the PI0.5 flow-matching VLA in both simulation and the real world. Most preference-learning methods only sharpen behaviors the policy already produces, so PrefPI's ability to reach genuinely out-of-distribution behaviors could let practitioners unlock new capabilities from existing pretrained policies with limited human feedback. This matters for robotics and preference-based learning researchers who want to avoid costly retraining or reward engineering. The method formulates preference learning as preference-conditioned generative modeling, where preferred trajectories define a conditional distribution whose density ratio with the broader behavior prior gives an implicit preference signal amplified by classifier-free guidance (CFG). Repeating this preference-conditioned modeling and guidance step yields a form of preference-guided policy iteration, though the approach still depends on the quality of the relative preference labels and the coverage of the behavior prior.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Generative robot policies, such as diffusion policies and flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models, learn to produce action sequences by sampling from a learned distribution, but they typically cannot generate behaviors far outside the data they were trained on. Preference learning lets humans compare trajectories instead of specifying numeric rewards, and classifier-free guidance is a standard diffusion-model technique that amplifies a conditional signal by contrasting it with an unconditional one. PrefPI combines these ideas to push a pretrained policy beyond its initial effective support.

## [MemLife Compacts Long-Term Egocentric Video into Retrievable Text Memories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40195) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MemLife introduces a multimodal memory system that converts long-term egocentric video into entity-grounded, first-person text episodes and retrieves them through a time-indexed agentic reader, without any training or query-time video access. It improves over the strongest training-free baseline by 4.6–12.0% across four long-horizon benchmarks, and the accompanying MemOpt reinforcement learning framework further boosts memory quality by 2.7–5.0%. As personal video histories grow to hundreds of hours, reprocessing raw clips for every query becomes computationally prohibitive, so a scalable memory layer is essential for personalized AI assistants that reason about daily life. MemLife shows that a training-free, text-based memory can outperform existing baselines, and MemOpt's gains generalize across writer and reader backbones, suggesting the approach could be widely adopted in multimodal assistant pipelines. The system avoids training and query-time video access entirely, instead compacting videos into entity-grounded text episodes that a time-indexed agentic reader can locate, addressing retrieval competition in growing search spaces. MemOpt is a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes the memory writer to produce faithful, informative, and retrievable memories, with improvements that hold across different video and question distributions.

The paper introduces SpeechConversationBench (SCB), a benchmark using 103 sharded GSM8K problems to evaluate spoken mathematical reasoning across three delivery conditions: full, concatenated, and incrementally sharded across turns. It reports that four commercial speech systems drop 5.0–25.3 percentage points in sharded accuracy versus concatenated, while a proprietary pipeline called LEGO maintains 77.5% accuracy in all three conditions, compared with 76.6% sharded accuracy for GPT-4o Realtime. The benchmark and the LEGO baseline provide a way to measure and improve robustness in voice agents, affecting developers building real-time speech interfaces. SCB uses 103 sharded GSM8K problems and compares final-answer accuracy across full, concat, and sharded conditions; the two single-turn baselines help separate sensitivity to problem reformulation from the added difficulty of incremental spoken interaction. LEGO is a proprietary speech pipeline developed by the SCBX Innovation Lab team with explicit conversational context management, and it achieves 77.5% accuracy in all three conditions.

The gains reportedly transfer beyond EviLens to WebEyes, conventional perception benchmarks, and general multimodal benchmarks, including a 15-point improvement on BrowseComp-VL. Agentic AI offers an alternative: an agent perceives its environment, decides what information is missing, and takes actions such as searching or zooming in to gather more evidence before answering. ## [ComputerSD: Online Self-Distillation for Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40253) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ComputerSD introduces an online self-distillation framework for computer-use agents (CUAs) that converts real-time feedback from executed GUI transitions into privileged guidance and step-level value scores, jointly optimizing token-level on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) and trajectory-level GRPO in a fully asynchronous training pipeline. On OSWorld-Verified, it outperforms outcome-only GRPO by 1.9 and 4.1 percentage points on Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking and EvoCUA-8B backbones respectively. Most CUA training relies on sparse outcome rewards that give no signal for intermediate actions, so this work shows how dense, real-time GUI feedback can be turned into token-level supervision that meaningfully improves policy learning. If it generalizes, it could make GUI automation agents more reliable and sample-efficient, benefiting developers building desktop and web automation systems. A fine-tuned GUI analyzer produces guidance and a step-level value score after each action; the guidance supplies privileged context while the score regulates the resulting OPSD signals, addressing the problems that fixed guidance can misalign with the student's current state and that guidance-induced probability shifts may conflict with step-level correctness. Evaluation in out-of-distribution settings further supports generalizability.

**Background**: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are AI systems that operate software through graphical user interfaces by simulating mouse and keyboard actions, and they are typically trained online by interacting with executable environments. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a technique in which a single model acts as both teacher and student with different contexts, giving dense token-level supervision by aligning the student's distribution with a teacher distribution conditioned on privileged information such as a verified solution. Reinforcement learning methods like GRPO, by contrast, optimize a trajectory-level objective from scalar outcome rewards, which is sparse for long GUI tasks.

A new arXiv paper (2609.40284) introduces cua-speedrun, a standardized benchmarking infrastructure and task set designed to reliably measure the speed and efficiency of computer-use agents (CUAs). It uses a uniform virtual machine setup, a shared execution pipeline, and a common agent interface that lets a single agent implementation run across four different CUA benchmarks, with all code and analysis released at cuaspeedrun.com. Speed and cost, not just task success, are now the main barriers to deploying CUAs in real-world settings, yet existing benchmarks are confounded by inconsistent machine and container configurations. By making speed comparisons reproducible across models, harnesses, and environments, cua-speedrun could give researchers and vendors a common yardstick for building faster, cheaper agents. Across four CUA benchmarks, the authors found that no single model family is best on performance, speed, and cost simultaneously, and that no open-weight model reaches the frontier. Counterintuitively, raising reasoning effort sped up task completion for some models, while faster environment input-output could actually slow overall task time; the team also showed most benchmark task sets can be shrunk without losing statistical power.

Researchers propose DynaHarness, a dynamic physical harness that couples a slow semantic "brain" with a fast execution "brain" through a shared execution contract, converting episode-level failure evidence into validated capability revisions. On LIBERO-Pro, it reaches 75.2% success on 800 newly sampled initial states versus 17.5% for the frozen policy, and 74.0% with full dynamic execution versus 63.9% under nominal one-step replanning. DynaHarness offers a governance layer that decides how existing capabilities are grounded, monitored, and coordinated, which could make pretrained VLA policies far more reliable without retraining the underlying model. The slow brain proposes capabilities with symbolic arguments, while the fast brain grounds and monitors commands, refuses unresolved actions, substitutes capabilities, and requests replans; a physical execution contract bounds each accepted command and records evidence across analytic skills, recovery skills, and a frozen VLA. Failure attribution localizes faults in these records, and paired regression checks govern whether revisions are admitted or rejected, closing the self-evolution loop.

## [Loop Scaling Laws Unify Recurrence and Sparsity for Looped MoE Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40316) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.40316) introduces Loop Scaling Laws, the first scaling law that jointly models recurrence and sparsity alongside model size and data. Its core is a bounded, sparsity-conditional recurrence mapping that quantifies the effective-parameter gain from looping and how sparsity increases that gain. The laws predict held-out loss of looped models more accurately than prior alternatives and recover standard dense and MoE scaling laws as special cases, giving researchers a principled foundation for designing looped MoE architectures under compute and memory constraints. Downstream evaluations show sparsity delivers roughly 3x active-parameter efficiency and recurrence yields about 2x total-parameter efficiency on reasoning, suggesting a practical path to more efficient large-model scaling. At matched training compute, a looped MoE with law-derived recurrence matches a roughly 2x larger non-looped MoE on reasoning benchmarks while enabling test-time scaling through recurrence, and these gains hold at trillion-token scale. The work is a cross-listed arXiv announcement and, as a scaling-law study, its predictions are empirical fits whose accuracy depends on the model and data regimes covered.

## [LLM Accuracy Collapses Super-Exponentially on Repetitive Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00763) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2511.00763v3) quantitatively studies how large language models perform on repetitive deterministic prediction tasks, such as letter replacement, integer addition, and string-operator multiplication in many-body quantum mechanics. The authors find that sequence accuracy rate (SAR) decays faster than exponential with output length N, collapsing sharply at a characteristic length N* — an 'accuracy cliff' — and that the hypothesis of independent per-step errors is rejected for every model and task tested. This work challenges the common assumption that per-step errors in LLM generation are independent, showing instead that errors accumulate through dense interactions, which has direct implications for how practitioners evaluate reliability and set safe output-length limits. The accuracy cliff suggests there is a predictable threshold beyond which LLM outputs become unreliable, affecting deployment of LLMs in long-sequence reasoning, code generation, and scientific computing. The crossover is well described by a double-exponential accumulation law, SAR = exp(−β₀ N α^{N−1}), whose crossover scale N* is independent of the fitting functional form. The authors introduce a minimal effective model with dense random couplings and an external field set by the prompt, which reproduces the super-linear error accumulation and assigns each model–task pair two interpretable parameters: an intrinsic error rate and an error-accumulation factor.

A new arXiv preprint (2511.22254v5) proposes a co-evolving framework in which a target agent and a dedicated failure agent improve together: the failure agent learns only from both agents' failed trajectories to generate higher-reward, plausible failures, which the target agent then uses as hard negatives for preference training. Across online shopping, scientific reasoning, and interactive SQL querying, the framework raises average task reward by 5.7 over the baseline, and the authors state the code will be made publicly available. This addresses a key limitation in self-improving agents: an agent's own obvious failures are easy to reject and provide weak supervision, so learning to generate plausible-but-wrong trajectories could substantially improve preference training. If the approach generalizes, it could influence how future agent systems mine their own experience for training signal. The failure agent is trained exclusively on failed trajectories from both agents and is rewarded for producing higher-reward failures, creating a feedback loop where target-policy improvement yields new failure data and the updated failure agent supplies fresh negatives. The reported 5.7 average reward gain is measured against a baseline across three distinct task domains, but the work is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

A new arXiv paper (2603.01209v3) studies 'runtime transfer' in CodeAct-style language-model agents, fine-tuning separate Qwen3-8B agents per task under persistent and stateless runtime contracts and evaluating all four training-deployment combinations. The findings show that fixed-runtime evaluations can conceal serious performance mismatches, meaning benchmark scores for fine-tuned agents may not transfer to real deployments with different runtime semantics. This has direct implications for how agent architectures are designed and how evaluations should report cost alongside quality. ## [ProjectMem: Local-First Event-Sourced Memory for AI Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12329) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ProjectMem introduces an open-source, local-first memory and judgment layer for AI coding agents that records development as an append-only, plain-text log of typed events (issues, attempts, fixes, decisions, notes) and deterministically projects it into compact summaries served through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). An author-run six-month self-study across two machines captured 3,228 unique events from 27 projects, and a synthetic-repository benchmark showed median analysis time for a 1,500-event log dropping from 42.0 seconds to 79.3 milliseconds. AI coding agents frequently lose project-specific rationale across sessions and repeat approaches that previously failed, and ProjectMem argues the real bottleneck is missing durable memory rather than model capability. By serving file-scoped advisory prechecks before edits — a design the authors call Memory-as-Governance — it offers a concrete, MCP-compatible path toward persistent project memory that could reduce repeated failures in tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Cline. The self-study found that 56% of events were issue-lifecycle events, and 86 of 427 distinct issues closed by a recorded fix had at least one failed attempt before the first fix in event-log order — though the authors caution these histories are candidates for later warnings, not evidence that warnings prevented failures. The benchmark also reduced git subprocesses per check from 1,500 to two while preserving the tested warning output, but the evaluation is limited to an author-run self-study and a synthetic repository, so generalizability remains unproven.

**Background**: Event sourcing is a pattern in which state is stored as an immutable, append-only sequence of events rather than as mutable records, allowing the current state to be reconstructed by replaying the log. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 that standardizes how LLM-based systems connect to external tools and data sources. ## [CombEval: A Dynamic Benchmark for Combinatorial Counting in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19788) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers released CombEval, a dynamic benchmark that represents each combinatorial counting problem as a typed Cofola specification over entities, objects, dependencies, and constraints, allowing controlled generation of natural-language problems with solver-verified exact answers. Evaluating 11 LLMs under direct and code-augmented settings, they found models remain brittle on ordered objects, indistinguishable elements, relatively positional constraints, and nested object dependencies. Combinatorial counting is a core reasoning skill that underlies probability, algorithm analysis, and many real-world planning tasks, so a diagnostic benchmark that pinpoints where and why LLMs fail provides actionable guidance for improving model reasoning. The finding that code augmentation does not fully resolve these failures suggests current tool-use strategies have limits for structured counting problems. Unlike static question banks, CombEval supports systematic variation of object type, entity scale, constraint count, and reasoning depth, and its error analysis identifies failures in constraint interpretation and counting principles. The code and generated benchmark suites are publicly available on GitHub.

**Background**: Combinatorial counting asks how many ways a set of objects can be arranged or selected under given constraints, and it is notoriously sensitive to subtle wording such as whether elements are distinguishable or ordered. Cofola is a declarative language and solver based on Weighted First-Order Model Counting (WFOMC) that lets users define sets, multisets, functions, and constraints and then automatically computes the number of solutions. CombEval builds on this by using Cofola specifications to generate natural-language counting problems with exact, solver-verified answers, enabling controlled and reproducible evaluation.

## [ORACLE: Adaptive Verifier Calibration for Agentic LLM Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22465) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ORACLE introduces a concurrency-aware, training-free online routing mechanism that first classifies task type and then dynamically assigns a task-appropriate verifier, replacing the fixed verifier used in prior serial verifier-based agentic routers. It also adds a delayed feedback strategy and a post-routing dispatch scheduler called DISC, which reserves each task's peak KV footprint at admission and reroutes to an alternate backend when reduced wait outweighs accuracy loss. Evaluated on SWE-bench, tau2-bench, and Terminal-Bench 2.0, ORACLE improves the accuracy-cost frontier by up to 7 percentage points over state-of-the-art routing baselines, and ORACLE with DISC raises program throughput by up to 1.8x. Enterprise agent deployments increasingly mix many LLMs of differing capability and cost, so routing decisions directly determine both serving quality and operating expense. By making verification adaptive and moving verifier latency off the dispatch critical path, ORACLE addresses two practical bottlenecks—heterogeneous task batches and concurrent request handling—that limit existing static and serial-verifier routers in production. ORACLE is training-free and acts as a drop-in feedback loop on top of any existing model-selection policy, so it does not require retraining the underlying router. Its delayed feedback strategy largely removes verifier latency from the dispatch critical path for concurrent requests, and DISC trades a controlled accuracy loss for reduced waiting by reserving peak KV cache footprint at admission and dispatching to an alternate backend.

**Background**: LLM routing is the practice of sending each query to the most suitable model from a pool, typically trading off answer quality against inference cost; frameworks such as RouteLLM and LLMRouter exemplify this approach. In agentic settings, a router may also invoke a verifier—a component that checks or scores a candidate answer—to provide feedback that guides task-level model selection. Prior verifier-based agentic routers used a single fixed verifier and placed it serially in the routing loop, which works for homogeneous workloads but can degrade quality and add latency when tasks are diverse or requests are concurrent.

A new arXiv paper (2607.22603v2) identifies a phenomenon called "group preference collapse," where multi-user personalized multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become insensitive to individual preferences and drift toward dominant population-level choices. To address this, the authors propose PrefMoE, a preference-centric framework that decomposes preferences into shared prototypes and personalized residuals and routes profile and preference factors through separate LoRA adaptation paths. The proposed framework could influence how future personalization systems are designed, particularly for applications serving diverse user populations. PrefMoE preserves individualized residuals using imbalance-aware learning, counterfactual pseudo-user augmentation, and residual decorrelation, and it separates stable profile information from preference-related representations. Experiments across multiple MLLM backbones show improved preference-sensitive personalization while substantially reducing preference collapse.

The pipeline produces 686K textbooks totaling 32B tokens across more than 15,000 disciplines; a content-matched Split condition (same text and tokens, but each section treated as an independent document) shows a +1.02 mean gain from document packaging alone, while a length-matched RandomConcat control that joins sections from different books remains below Full, ruling out document length as the sole explanation. A retrieval-pool-matched Rephrase condition that independently rewrites individual retrieved documents without clustering, TOC planning, or book assembly yields a +1.17 gain for Full, and on Llama3-8B, Full also outperforms both RandomConcat and Natural Books.

## [Fast LapSum Achieves Exact Differentiable Top-k at Million Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06912) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Fast LapSum introduces a scalable solver for the LapSum soft top-k formulation that preserves an exact selection mass of k while supporting end-to-end differentiation. It uses probabilistic bracketing with a binomial order-statistic to restrict sorting to a narrow band around the threshold, and a certification pass upgrades this to a verified localization with a full-sort fallback. The certified GPU implementation processes 10^6, 10^7, and 10^8 scores in median times of 0.92 ms, 1.39 ms, and 7.24 ms, respectively. Differentiable top-k is a fundamental operation for inducing sparsity in large-scale models, enabling expert activation, token routing, and attention pruning, but existing differentiable alternatives become increasingly expensive as the number of coordinates grows. Fast LapSum makes exact-budget soft top-k practical within million-scale optimization loops, with demonstrated order-of-magnitude speedup in megapixel sparse adversarial examples and significant computation reduction in 3D Gaussian splatting. The method reduces sorting cost by using a binomial order-statistic from kernel-noised samples to localize the threshold, then a certification pass verifies the localization at the cost of one additional linear pass, with a full-sort fallback covering worst-case scenarios. In 3D Gaussian splatting, Fast LapSum reduces the number of Gaussians produced by Adaptive Density Control while retaining nearly the same rendering quality.

## [SAPO Unifies Policy and Value Learning in a Single LLM for Agentic RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19842) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SAPO (Single-rollout Autoregressive Policy Optimization) is a new PPO-style framework that unifies policy optimization and value learning inside a single causal language model, generating actions and value estimates sequentially at distinct causal boundaries with shared parameters. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B and Qwen3-14B show SAPO cuts peak GPU memory by 23.1% and per-iteration runtime by 24.8% versus a strong PPO baseline, while matching or slightly improving task success and beating GRPO and recent variants in stability. Agentic RL is a key post-training route for improving LLM agents, but existing methods force a trade-off between policy quality and resource cost: PPO needs a separate critic that consumes large memory, while critic-free group-relative methods like GRPO need multiple rollouts and can struggle on long-horizon tasks. By removing the separate critic and the multi-rollout requirement at once, SAPO could make agentic RL post-training cheaper and more stable for practitioners working with limited GPU budgets. SAPO jointly optimizes the standard PPO objective with an auxiliary on-policy SARSA objective using turn-level generalized advantage estimation, where the SARSA term is designed to facilitate value learning; the value head is not a separate network but shares parameters with the policy inside one causal LM. Evaluation is limited to two text-based agent benchmarks (ALFWorld and WebShop) and Qwen-family models, so generalization to other model families, modalities, or longer-horizon environments remains to be verified.

Critic-free group-relative methods such as GRPO instead estimate advantages from reward statistics across a group of sampled responses for the same prompt, avoiding the critic but requiring multiple rollouts per prompt. SARSA is a classic on-policy RL algorithm that updates value estimates using the actually taken next action, in contrast to off-policy Q-learning.
