## [CONTRAMEM Builds Training-Free Procedural Memory for Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22533) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CONTRAMEM is a source-flexible, training-free framework that constructs self-evolving procedural memory for autonomous computer-use agents by contrasting multi-model trajectories on the same tasks, distilling differences in correctness, efficiency, recovery, and failure modes into app-level Function Cards and task-level Skill Cards. On held-out GAIA2/ARE computer-use tasks it more than doubles success rates across three source-model targets (26.2% to 55.3%), with per-model gains such as GPT-5.5 rising from 27.5 to 61.0 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 from 28.0 to 52.5. This matters because it shows high-quality procedural memory for agents can be built without any model training, using contrastive behavioral diversity from heterogeneous models rather than stronger source agents or more sampling. The resulting memory bank transfers unchanged to an unseen model (Qwen3.7 Plus, 18.5 to 35.5) and to a different benchmark (AppWorld), suggesting transferable procedural knowledge rather than model-specific behavior. The memory bank evolves through localized curation rather than append-only accumulation or whole-bank rewriting, and under a matched trajectory budget heterogeneous multi-model trajectories outperform self- or same-model multi-rollout memory. The same construction carries over unchanged to AppWorld, beating both no memory and its own single-source self-memory variant for all three mid-tier agents on both public test splits.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Autonomous computer-use agents handle long-horizon tasks that require coordinated application calls, persistent state tracking, and verifier-sensitive writes, but they often fail procedurally by misreading application state, tool semantics, or task progress. Procedural memory — analogous to the human memory of skills and habits — promises more consistent decisions and less redundant exploration, yet building high-quality memory without model training remains difficult. CONTRAMEM addresses this by treating same-task outcome variation across different models as a supervision signal, distilling it into compact Function Cards and Skill Cards.

## [AtlasNav Builds Persistent Corpus Atlas to Curb Evidence Blindness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24764) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.24764v2) introduces AtlasNav, a persistent multi-view Corpus Atlas that pre-organizes cross-document structure before any query arrives, so language-model agents can navigate evidence adaptively instead of reconstructing search directions at query time. On BrowseComp-Plus with DeepSeek as the backbone, AtlasNav improves strict accuracy by 7.47 points while cutting query-time inference cost by 30.22% compared with the previous state-of-the-art interactive corpus access method. As LLM agents shift from retrieval-augmented generation toward direct corpus interaction, the bottleneck is no longer access but whether usable evidence can be found within a finite interaction budget; AtlasNav reframes this as a structural pre-organization problem rather than a per-query search problem. If the gains hold across backbones and domains, it could change how agentic research systems are architected for enterprise and web-scale corpora. The Corpus Atlas organizes every canonical file once through four complementary views—Topic, Identity, Episode, and Relation—and trains a lightweight query-adaptive Router that combines these semantic channels with BM25, while the full corpus remains directly searchable and openable. The paper reports that AtlasNav reduces Evidence Blindness, surfaces complete evidence earlier, stays robust to corpus-structure and scale shifts on PhantomWiki, and achieves leading performance on heterogeneous enterprise data.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) traditionally fetches a fixed set of passages per query, but newer language-model agents instead interact directly with a corpus—searching, opening documents, and following newly discovered evidence iteratively. This direct corpus interaction (DCI) keeps the whole corpus reachable, yet under a finite interaction budget agents may never see, open, or extract decisive evidence from the right documents, a failure mode the authors call Evidence Blindness. AtlasNav addresses this by pre-building reusable cross-document structure, analogous to a map of the corpus, rather than leaving structure implicit or rebuilding it at query time.

A new arXiv paper (2609.00455v2) proposes Belief-Based World Models (BB-WMs), which maintain a belief state that LLM agents can query in natural language to access what is known and uncertain about the current state. Experiments show that exposing this belief directly to an LLM policy improves task performance under partial observability and is complementary to existing simulation-based world models, with code released at github.com/skumar-ml/belief-world-models. If validated, BB-WMs could become a standard component for planning and decision-making in robotics, games, and other partially observable domains. The paper focuses on the fundamental question of whether exposing a world model's belief directly to an LLM policy helps decision-making, rather than on learning accurate BB-WMs, and the authors built benchmark-specific instantiations while leaving scalable, domain-agnostic learning methods for future work. It is an arXiv preprint without peer review, so the reported gains have not yet been independently verified.

## [DiagEvo: Diagnosis-Guided Self-Evolution for Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00768) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced DiagEvo, a diagnosis-guided self-evolution method that uses a solver's failure history from self-play to generate targeted questions without external task resources. With a default 4B diagnostician, it outperforms all baselines across nine benchmarks for Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and OctoThinker-8B, reaching 72.3% mean accuracy on five math reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3-8B, 4.5 points above R-Zero. This work addresses a key limitation of self-play training, where solver performance can plateau or decline across rounds without guidance, and it removes the reliance on external task resources like human examples or document corpora. If validated, it could make autonomous curriculum learning for language models more effective and self-contained, benefiting researchers working on reasoning improvement. The diagnostician extracts recurring error causes into an error-cause memory, grouping related causes under skill nodes tracked as Active or Mastered based on self-consistency on targeted questions, while a challenger balances cause-targeted generation with free exploration. Double-confidence filtering retains intermediate-difficulty questions only when the most common solver answer has a clear vote lead, and ablations confirm that mixed generation, memory-state updates with cross-state stitching, and double-confidence filtering all contribute to the gains.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Self-play is a paradigm where a language model generates its own training questions and iteratively solves them, enabling self-evolution without human supervision. Unguided methods steer question generation using signals like difficulty, learnability, or diversity, but they do not identify which specific reasoning weaknesses to target, while guided methods typically depend on external resources such as human examples or document corpora. Self-consistency refers to generating multiple reasoning paths and selecting the answer by majority vote, a technique used here to judge whether a skill has been mastered.

## [ResidualAuth formalizes authorization state for revocable agent delegation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08062) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ResidualAuth introduces a formal framework, centered on the "residual authorization state," that equates two delegation histories exactly when every future sequence of grants, revocations, and uses is valid after both or neither. The paper proves exponentially many distinct residual states can share one fixed transitive closure, derives exact or tight memory bounds as delegation redundancy varies, and reports an average decision-error lower bound under a bound on retained information, plus an executable benchmark where four open-weight models scored 15-16/16 correct pairs with trusted Allow/Deny decisions versus 0-2/16 with event extracts alone. Tool-using language agents increasingly delegate and revoke permissions through external services, and this work shows that identical current permissions can still require opposite decisions after the same revocation, meaning systems that store only current permission state are fundamentally unsafe. It gives agent and authorization-infrastructure builders a formal target for what state must be retained, plus a benchmark for testing whether models can actually use that state. The framework separates three questions that are often conflated: whether relevant information is accessible, whether online state can be maintained across updates, and whether available information is actually used to make correct decisions. Diagnostics found that models produced invalid reconstructions of memory, and also answered incorrectly from valid memories that nonetheless passed fixed future authorization tests, indicating that passing a static test does not guarantee correct authorization reasoning.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: In delegation, one principal authorizes another (for example, a user authorizes an agent, which authorizes a sub-agent) to act using some of the delegator's rights; revocation withdraws that authority. Because revocation is not simply the inverse of granting, the history of grants and revocations can matter even when the current set of permissions looks the same. ResidualAuth formalizes exactly which distinctions in that history must be preserved for future authorization decisions to remain correct.

## [JustFit Brings Just-in-Time State Management to Local LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17475) ⭐️ 7.0/10

JustFit is an MLX runtime that coordinates overlapping memory allocations for model execution and working history, combining KVExec (four-bit KV execution and checkpointing with bounded workspace), PhaseSwap (loading phase-dependent components), and StateTrans (preserving history across execution modes). On a 24 GiB M4 Pro MacBook running Qwen3.8-27B MXFP4, it retains 327,680 positions across two requests — 10.67x the evaluated baseline's 30,720-position single-request record — and completes a full 262,144-position native window at a median 5.986 tokens/s. Long-context local inference is usually bottlenecked by KV cache memory rather than raw compute, so a 10.67x increase in retained positions on consumer hardware could make much longer agent histories and documents feasible on personal laptops. This matters for the local inference and Apple-silicon communities, where MLX is the primary framework for running models on unified memory. Each shape completes 16,384 outputs per request across three fresh processes, with B1 using one cold build plus two prefix extensions and B2 using three ordered prefix extensions; image encoding can proceed while preserving a live 196,608-input text request. A controlled repetitive 32K+6K workload reaches a median 18.284 tokens/s at 15,626 MiB, and a separate AIME 2026 evaluation scores 29/30.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: MLX is Apple's open-source array framework for machine learning on Apple silicon, optimized for the unified memory architecture so the CPU and GPU can share data without copying. During autoregressive LLM decoding, the KV cache stores key and value tensors for all previous tokens, and its memory footprint grows with context length, making it a major bottleneck for long-context serving. MXFP4 is a 4-bit floating-point quantization format that shrinks model weights and cache memory, while still requiring careful handling of scale factors.

## [SCLATE: A Unified Substrate for Continual-Learning Agent Training and Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32391) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SCLATE is an execution substrate that lets benchmarks and unmodified agents each register their events into a single open event scheduler through an adapter, using a hybrid simulated clock that flows in real time while the agent works and skips idle gaps. The authors ported seven benchmarks to SCLATE, compared ten unmodified harness and memory configurations across ten models, and post-trained Qwen3.5-4B to read 6.8x fewer file lines with a 16.7-point higher SWE-bench Verified pass rate. Continual-learning agents operate over long multi-session horizons, but existing benchmarks and training frameworks only schedule their own events, forcing every benchmark-agent pair to build a custom scheduling loop. SCLATE addresses this infrastructure gap by unifying event scheduling, which could make multi-session agent evaluation and training far more reproducible and efficient for researchers. The hybrid simulated clock compresses a month-long scenario into hours, and SCLATE also acts as a rollout engine that runs any agent's harness and memory unmodified while recording the tokens and log probabilities of every model call through an in-container proxy. Notably, the comparison found that an added memory system does not reliably beat the harness's native memory, and models differ widely in how they use the same harness and memory.

## [TRACE Self-Calibrates Wireless Digital Twins from RF Measurements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32923) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce TRACE (Twin Residual Alignment and Calibration Engine), a physics-grounded learning framework that repairs wireless digital twins by treating twin maintenance as residual alignment between measured and simulated RF signals. On 5,400 held-out samples from unseen simulated scenes at 28 GHz, TRACE cuts 3D position RMSE from 2.202 m to 0.302 m and yaw RMSE from 4.978° to 0.894°, and on measured NIST outdoor courtyard data it reduces mean planar wall-position error from 1.00 m to 7.8 cm without any measured-data fine-tuning or geometric labels. Wireless digital twins are increasingly used to plan and optimize network deployments, but their accuracy is limited by imperfect 3D maps of buildings, so errors in position, height, footprint, and orientation cause high-fidelity propagation engines to simulate the wrong physical environment. TRACE shows that a deployed network's own RF measurements can serve as a learning signal to repair the twin, potentially reducing manual surveying and maintenance costs for operators and enabling more reliable coverage and localization decisions. TRACE ray-traces the current twin using the same sensing configuration as the physical measurements, coherently backprojects measured and simulated RF onto a common world grid, and extracts identical local regions around each building's current twin position. A multi-view corrector then fuses evidence across sensing nodes and neighboring buildings to predict a gated six-parameter correction per building without relying on absolute layout or sensor ordering, and supports iterative correction through re-rendering; it outperforms ViT and U-Net baselines under changes in layout, building count, sensing-node count, and SNR.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: A wireless digital twin is a software replica of a physical wireless environment, typically built from 3D environment models, that predicts radio propagation to support network planning and optimization. Ray tracing is a deterministic simulation method that computes propagation paths from 3D geometry and electromagnetic properties, so its accuracy depends heavily on the quality of the underlying environment model. ISAC (Integrated Sensing and Communication) refers to wireless systems that use the same waveform and protocol for both sensing and communication, which is relevant because TRACE exploits a network's own sensing/measurement capability to calibrate its twin.

## [CompoWorld Scales Cross-Service Environments to Train General Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33665) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CompoWorld introduces Compositional Environment Scaling, a method that composes a finite library of reusable services into cross-service tasks for training general agents. It builds 448 services exposing 10,130 tools, uses coding agents to generate verified services with typed states and shared interfaces, and relies on a world model for tools that cannot be reliably implemented, training Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with 3K SFT trajectories and 1K RL tasks to achieve a 9.17-point average gain across eight benchmarks. Most existing environment-generation approaches only create tasks within a single environment, which fails to reflect real-world workflows where agents must connect information and actions across multiple services. By scaling task space through service composition, CompoWorld offers a more realistic and scalable path to training general agents, and its results on AutomationBench surpass frontier models such as Claude Opus 4.6. The framework uses a random-walk procedure over dependency graphs to connect services and verify tasks requiring cross-service information flow; verified trajectories feed supervised fine-tuning, while a Completion-Focused Rubric Reward guides RL by emphasizing criteria with lower pass rates within each rollout group. The world model is a fallback for tools that cannot be reliably implemented as real services, which is a notable limitation since simulated tools may not perfectly match real behavior.

## [Stratified Inoculation Prompting Reduces Backdoors, Keeps Desired Traits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35356) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Stratified Inoculation Prompting (SIP), which uses a small clean subset of training examples to oversample desired behavior under diverse non-eliciting prompts while applying the inoculation prompt to the rest. SIP substantially reduces undesired behavior expression and preserves more desired behavior than standard Inoculation Prompting (IP), and it also yields lower emergent misalignment rates across all harmful-advice setups tested. This work addresses a key limitation of IP, where undesired behavior can still leak under unrelated prompts and desired behavior learning can be hindered, making it relevant for AI safety and fine-tuning practitioners who need selective generalization. The extensions backdoor dilution and password-locked inoculation further show promise for controlling behavior even when the undesired trait is explicitly requested. SIP oversamples clean examples under diverse non-eliciting prompts while inoculating the rest, and its gains persist even when IP is extended to oversample the same clean subset at the same rate. The paper also introduces backdoor dilution, which weakens expression under the inoculation prompt, and password-locked inoculation, which concentrates elicitation on a designated password.

The paper introduces a fixed-rollout counterfactual diagnostic that separates Evidence-Function Sensitivity (EFS) from claim persistence, revealing that under DAPO and VPPO, unsupported visual claims become significantly more persistent even as EFS increases. The proposed diagnostic and PACG method offer a practical, label-free way to improve multimodal credit assignment, likely influencing future perception-aware RL research and hallucination mitigation. Before RL training, 27.81% of correctly answered responses from Qwen2.5-VL-7B on four multimodal reasoning benchmarks contain at least one direct visual claim unsupported by the image. The diagnostic reveals Sensitivity-Persistence Decoupling (SPD): DAPO and VPPO increase EFS but make unsupported claims more persistent, whereas GRPO raises EFS without this deterioration; PACG also improves HallusionBench accuracy and generalizes to a larger model and newer backbone.

## [BudgetPM: Budgeting External State Checks for Agent Prospective Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37125) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces BudgetPM, the first resource-allocation formulation for the external observations that stored intentions require under a shared episode budget, offering two policy variants (BudgetPM-Static and BudgetPM-Sequential) that share a hard-budget executor. Evaluated against two public memory-agent systems, five matched controls, and four hand-designed rules across two benchmarks and three backbones, BudgetPM-Static retains 99.9–100% of unconstrained quality with 42–54% fewer observations, while BudgetPM-Sequential beats the strongest tested natural monitoring schedule by 1.92–2.58 Set F1 points under severe scarcity. Prospective memory — retaining an intention tied to a future condition — is a core capability for tool-augmented LLM agents, but checking whether that condition holds can require web access, multi-step tool use, and paid API calls. By treating these checks as a budgeted resource rather than a free action, BudgetPM offers a demand–capacity design rule that could reduce cost and latency in deployed agent memory systems. BudgetPM-Static uses a lightweight Logistic scorer to learn whether a check improves the current decision, while BudgetPM-Sequential distills full-episode hindsight schedules into a lightweight policy that decides when to spend or reserve capacity using only pre-query information at deployment. Matched attribution, exact-cost analysis, and a fixed-budget load intervention link the gains to competition between present and future opportunities, yielding the rule that local gating works when capacity covers demand, while future-aware supervision adds value when observations compete across time.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Prospective memory in AI agents refers to the ability to carry out a deferred intention at the right future cue while other activities continue, a skill isolated by benchmarks such as PM-Bench. Existing memory-agent systems decide when stored intentions require attention, but they do not allocate the resulting observations under a shared budget, even though each check may involve costly tool calls. BudgetPM addresses this gap by formulating the problem as resource allocation over a fixed episode budget.

## [SimpleEvol: An Agent-Loop Framework for LLM-Driven Automated Heuristic Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37172) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes SimpleEvol, an agent-loop framework for automated heuristic design (AHD) that removes nearly all human priors and lets the LLM operate autonomously, alongside two new metrics: AHI (framework handcraftedness) and ICE (intelligence conversion efficiency). Evaluating ten LLMs across three challenging combinatorial optimization problems, the authors find that frameworks with fewer human priors consistently yield higher ICE, and SimpleEvol achieves the highest ICE, often by a large margin. This work challenges the dominant paradigm of embedding LLMs as narrow, fixed components (e.g., crossover or mutation) inside heavily hand-engineered evolutionary pipelines, arguing such designs violate the 'bitter lesson' principle. If validated, it points toward lighter, more model-centric AHD frameworks that scale with model intelligence, which could reshape how researchers build AI-for-optimization systems. The framework is evaluated on three challenging combinatorial optimization problems using ten different LLMs, and the source code is released at https://github.com/HenryZhu1029/SimpleEvol-Master. The key empirical claim is that reducing human priors is a more effective strategy for scaling with model intelligence than adding hand-crafted pipeline complexity.

The 'bitter lesson,' proposed by Richard Sutton in 2019, observes that general methods which scale with computation tend to outperform approaches built on domain-specific human knowledge in the long run. ## [TopK SAE Reliability: Active Budget k Kills Rare-Feature Sensitivity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37857) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.37857v2) diagnoses why scaling TopK sparse autoencoders selectively degrades the sensitivity of rare features, identifying the active budget k as the root cause through a controlled width×k factorial experiment. The authors propose pairwise rank stabilization, which improves rare-feature sensitivity by 8.83 percentage points while keeping reconstruction and alive-feature coverage near baseline. Sparse autoencoders are a core tool for mechanistic interpretability of large language models, and this work shows that wider dictionaries can silently erode the reliability of rare features that researchers depend on for stable interpretation. It argues that SAEs should be evaluated not only by reconstruction, sparsity, and feature count, but also by feature reliability under semantic variation and boundary geometry. The degradation stems from the selection boundary of TopK rather than dictionary width alone, and the paper introduces the active margin — the distance to the cutoff — as a threshold-free predictor of feature loss. Pairwise rank stabilization specifically targets ordering failures at the cutoff, improving rare-feature sensitivity by 8.83 percentage points without materially hurting reconstruction or alive-feature coverage.

## [SelfSearch: Reward-Free Self-Improvement for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37968) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SelfSearch introduces a reward-free search procedure in which LLM agents improve themselves by learning from records of previous self-modification episodes, capturing the reasoning, tool actions, and outcomes of earlier attempts. Across all six model-benchmark settings the population-mean success improves over the initial agent, with individual agents gaining up to 11.2 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 5.0 points on SWE-bench Multilingual while cutting execution cost by 38.5% on tasks solved by both versions. This matters because existing self-improving agent methods rely on repeated downstream evaluation, which is expensive and ties the search to specific tasks; removing the reward signal could make agent self-evolution cheaper and more general. The reported result that a harness produced for only $4.03 matches the top-scoring Codex harness on Terminal-Bench 2.1 suggests reward-free search may become a practical alternative to evaluation-guided pipelines. The method works without any downstream reward signal during search, yet remains competitive with evaluation-guided search baselines at lower search cost. Notably, the $4.03 harness solves 82.0% of Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks with DeepSeek V4 Flash under the settings of a public nine-harness comparison, though the abstract is truncated and full methodological details are limited in the provided content.

## [KV-Kaizen Learns Context-Adaptive Per-Layer KV Cache Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37988) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.37988v2) introduces KV-Kaizen, a method that learns a selector producing a per-layer KV cache configuration along three axes — cross-layer sharing (depth), bit precision, and low-rank truncation — to meet an overall compression budget without evicting any tokens. The selector runs once before pre-fill, and on long-context tasks it reaches a 32x smaller decode-time cache on a 14B model while preserving accuracy, with a 4x reduction causing no degradation from 7B parameters up. KV cache memory is a first-order bottleneck for long-context LLM inference, and existing solutions mostly evict tokens, which risks permanently discarding information that later turns out to be relevant. By compressing instead of evicting and by composing depth, precision, and rank choices adaptively per layer, KV-Kaizen points toward cheaper long-context serving and supports a pre-train-large-then-compress workflow. The paper reports that applying these interventions independently and uniformly across all layers limits achievable compression because it degrades accuracy, whereas composing them locally and adaptively preserves accuracy while saving large amounts of memory. On instruction-following and reasoning benchmarks the selectors reach the Pareto frontier of accuracy versus cache size against learning-free and post-hoc baselines, and the method can be composed with token eviction; a compressed model is also more accurate than a smaller uncompressed model with the same cache size.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Transformer-based LLMs store key and value tensors for every past token in a KV cache so that autoregressive decoding does not have to recompute them, but this cache grows linearly with context length and can exceed the memory used by the model weights themselves. Because decoding is memory-bound, a larger cache directly lowers throughput. Prior work attacks this with eviction (dropping least-relevant tokens), quantization (storing caches at fewer bits), low-rank projection (caching compressed latent representations), or cross-layer sharing, but usually applies one strategy uniformly across all layers.

## [ETHER Uses Emergent Communication to Fix Hindsight Experience Replay for Instruction-Following RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15494) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces ETHER (Emergent Textual Hindsight Experience Replay), an agent that uses a referential game to train a speaker and listener to develop a grounded artificial language describing environment states. It partially aligns this emergent language with task instructions via co-occurrence patterns, and experiments on BabyAI's PickupDist task show that the learned speaker and listener can serve as HER's goal relabelling and predicate functions, improving sample efficiency despite imperfect alignment. This work bridges emergent communication and goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, addressing a fundamental limitation of HER in instruction-following tasks where goals are expressed in natural language and differ from the state space. It opens the door to wider applications of HER in language-conditioned RL, potentially benefiting researchers working on sample-efficient learning with sparse rewards. ETHER formalizes the Hindsight Reinforcement Learning problem, which requires jointly learning goal relabelling and predicate functions alongside the RL policy. The approach uses a referential game to develop an emergent language and aligns it with instructions using co-occurrence patterns, but the alignment is imperfect, which may limit performance in more complex tasks.

## [Distribution Matching Framework Unifies Self-Supervised Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14424) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2502.14424v5) formulates self-supervised representation learning as Distribution Matching (DM), where an augmentation-invariant encoder is trained so its induced distribution matches an explicit geometric reference law, using Mallows distance as the discrepancy measure. The authors prove a non-asymptotic neural-sieve guarantee and connect the population objective to class-centre separation and classification error, with simulations and image benchmarks showing manifold rectification, fine-grained structure, and transfer across label spaces. Most self-supervised learning methods focus on preventing representation collapse but leave the target representation distribution unspecified; this work provides a principled target law and theoretical guarantees, potentially offering a more interpretable and transferable foundation for representation learning. It could influence how future SSL objectives are designed and how transfer learning across label spaces is approached. The framework separates the reference law (what the representation distribution should look like) from the discrepancy measure (how deviations are quantified), using Mallows distance here; the authors establish a directional inverse relationship with generative learning, where generative models map a tractable reference to data while representation learning maps data to a designed reference. The non-asymptotic neural-sieve guarantee provides finite-sample theoretical support, though empirical validation is currently limited to simulations and standard image benchmarks.

Mallows distance (a form of Wasserstein distance) measures the cost of transforming one probability distribution into another, and neural-sieve theory studies the approximation and generalization properties of neural networks as the number of parameters grows.

## [AneumoBench: A Source-Linked Benchmark for Aneurysm CFD Surrogate Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14717) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers released AneumoBench, a dataset and benchmark that links 401 source aneurysm geometries to 9,693 locally edited descendant records, with CFD fields computed on both. It contains 80,752 steady velocity-pressure cases across eight inlet conditions and 9,715 transient sequences of velocity, pressure, and wall shear stress (WSS), each with 100 frames sampled at 0.01-s intervals from a 1-s cardiac cycle. This benchmark enables controlled, family-disjoint evaluation of whether synthetic geometry variants actually improve surrogate model prediction on unseen aneurysm geometries, a question central to scientific machine learning for hemodynamics. It provides a shared protocol for comparing descendant selection and training strategies, which could accelerate the development of fast, clinically relevant CFD surrogates. The benchmark offers mesh, point, and voxel interfaces for steady field prediction and WSS forecasting from four observed frames, and compares source-only training, descendant training, and descendant pretraining followed by source fine-tuning across nine architectures on 79 held-out sources. Under the reported schedules, two-stage training lowers steady-field and reset-window WSS errors, but reset-window gains do not consistently persist through 96-step rollout, and lower trajectory error need not improve cycle-level shear metrics or hotspot localization.

The paper introduces CLVQ-VAE, a cross-layer vector-quantized variational autoencoder that maps lower-layer representations to higher layers through a discrete quantization bottleneck, collapsing duplicated residual-stream features into compact, interpretable concept vectors. It combines top-k temperature-based sampling with exponential moving average (EMA) codebook updates, and outperforms clustering, single-layer VQ-VAE, and sparse autoencoder baselines on ERASER-Movie, Jigsaw, and AGNews across three evaluation axes. This work addresses a key limitation in mechanistic interpretability: the residual stream linearly mixes and duplicates features across adjacent layers, causing single-layer analyses to miss cross-layer structure. The method uses a discrete vector-quantization bottleneck with top-k temperature-based sampling and EMA codebook updates to maintain codebook diversity. Evaluation shows that removing identified concepts drops downstream probe accuracy by up to 93%, LLM judges rank the concepts first in 66.7% of comparisons, and human annotators recover model predictions from visualizations with 78% accuracy versus 54% for clustering.

PRI incrementally detaches important patches while allowing others to continue evolving, achieving up to 10x faster inversion than Dense Model Inversion (DMI) and 2x faster than SMI, with better accuracy than SMI and matching DMI. The method achieves these speedups while maintaining accuracy, but as a preprint, it has not yet undergone peer review.

## [TRAAC: RL Method Balances Under- and Overthinking in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01581) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers released TRAAC (Think Right with Adaptive, Attentive Compression), an online post-training reinforcement learning method that uses the model's own self-attention to identify key reasoning steps and prune redundant ones, while estimating task difficulty to allocate reasoning budgets accordingly. On AIME, AMC, GPQA-D, and BBEH, TRAAC applied to Qwen3-4B achieved an average absolute accuracy gain of 8.4% with a 36.8% relative reduction in reasoning length versus the base model, and a 7.9% accuracy gain with a 29.4% shorter output versus the best RL baseline. As reasoning models scale test-time compute, they often waste tokens on easy problems (overthinking) or fail on hard ones (underthinking); TRAAC shows that difficulty-aware reward design plus attention-based step pruning can improve both accuracy and token efficiency simultaneously. This matters for anyone deploying reasoning LLMs, since shorter, better-calibrated chains of thought directly reduce inference cost and latency. TRAAC is an online post-training RL method that combines two signals: self-attention weights used to detect and prune redundant reasoning steps, and a difficulty estimate folded into the training reward so the model learns a reasoning budget commensurate with each example. Gains also generalize to out-of-distribution, non-math benchmarks such as GPQA-D, BBEH, and OptimalThinkingBench, though results are reported on a single 4B-scale model (Qwen3-4B) and the paper is an arXiv preprint.

Reinforcement learning post-training is a common way to shape such model behavior, and prior work has shown that attention weights can signal which reasoning steps are critical versus redundant.

## [Instruction Retrieval Boosts Small Language Models at Inference Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13935) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2510.13935v3) introduces 'instruction retrieval,' a method that distills a teacher model's expertise into a reusable corpus of domain-specific instructions, which a frozen small language model retrieves and follows at inference time without any fine-tuning. On the MedQA benchmark, this corpus raises mean accuracy by 10.6 points, compared to only 3.9 points from retrieved textbook passages and a decrease when using few-shot examples from the same teacher. This approach enables small language models on edge devices to handle expert tasks in medicine, law, and mathematics without costly per-domain fine-tuning, potentially democratizing access to specialized AI on resource-constrained hardware. It also offers a more efficient alternative to retrieval-augmented generation by retrieving procedural guidance and background knowledge rather than raw passages. The instruction corpus is built once per domain by having the teacher model write, for each cluster of problems, one instruction containing background knowledge, a procedure, and common mistakes; at inference, the frozen small model retrieves the nearest instructions. Error analysis shows that background knowledge fixes questions the small model always gets wrong, while procedure and common mistakes fix only questions where it wavers between options.

EDGC combines efficient entropy estimation via gradient sampling, a theoretical model linking entropy to compression rank under a bounded-error constraint, and window-based rank adjustment across pipeline stages. A new arXiv paper (2602.01687v3) hypothesizes that large language models create functional subspaces in their activation space and use vector algebra within those subspaces to solve tasks. By analyzing functional modules and residual streams during in-context learning, the authors find evidence that LLMs can accumulate evidence in subspaces and solve ICL tasks via simple algebraic operations. This work offers a mechanistic explanation for in-context learning, one of the most important emergent abilities of LLMs, and could improve model interpretability, diagnostics, and repair. The paper builds on prior work showing that high-level concepts are encoded as linear directions in activation space, but it does not yet provide a full causal validation or a practical tool for practitioners.

## [ResidualKV Compresses KV Cache via Sparse References and Quantized Residuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08005) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2602.08005v2) introduces ResidualKV, a KV cache compression method that factorizes the cache into a sparse set of globally retrieved references plus compact, quantized residual codes for the remaining tokens. Across Llama, Qwen, LLaVA-OV, and Qwen3-VL backbones, it retains near-full-cache performance using only 13%-16% KV storage and 30% attention computation on LongBench, with up to 3.4x decoding speedup without quantization. KV cache memory grows linearly with context length while attention computation grows quadratically, making long-context inference a major bottleneck for multi-turn dialogue and long-form reasoning. ResidualKV avoids irreversible token eviction, so it could let practitioners serve much longer contexts on existing hardware without permanently losing token-specific information. The method is motivated by two empirical properties, Long-Range Inter-Token Similarity and Smooth Residual Distribution, and uses dynamic-stride scheduling to reduce reference growth from linear to approximately logarithmic at ultra-long contexts. In matched-budget multimodal evaluation it achieves 8%-10% storage and 10% computation, and it accelerates decoding up to 1.5x with KV-cache quantization; the source code is available on GitHub.

**Background**: In Transformer-based large language models, the KV cache stores key and value vectors for all previously processed tokens so that generation does not need to recompute them, but its memory footprint scales linearly with sequence length. Sparse attention reduces the quadratic cost of attention by letting each query attend to only a subset of keys and values, while residual vector quantization approximates vectors as the sum of codewords from successive codebooks. ResidualKV combines these ideas to compress the cache without permanently discarding tokens.

A new arXiv paper (2602.13194v3) introduces a statistical framework that uses large language models to recursively segment text into semantically coherent chunks, forming a 'semantic tree' that spans from main ideas down to individual tokens. The authors define a 'structural' entropy rate from these trees and find it closely matches LLM-measured entropy across corpora, with simpler texts like children's stories showing lower branching and entropy than fiction and poetry. This work offers a fresh bridge between classic information theory and modern NLP, suggesting that the hierarchical semantic organization of text is a key driver of its overall information transmission rate. It could influence how researchers think about redundancy, compression, and semantic chunking strategies used in retrieval-augmented generation and other LLM applications. The framework recursively segments any given text using LLMs to induce semantic trees, and for a large corpus of a particular type the ensemble of trees exhibits specific statistical regularities. The measured semantic tree entropy rate was surprisingly close to the LLM-measured quantity and showed similar trends across datasets, though the study focuses on several specific corpora rather than all text types.

Semantic chunking, the practice of splitting text into meaning-based segments, is widely used in NLP and LLM pipelines for tasks like retrieval-augmented generation.

MoEless introduces optimized scaling and placement strategies to improve function locality, GPU utilization, and cross-expert load balance, avoiding costly expert swapping or degraded output quality. ## [Semi-DPO Uses Semi-Supervised Learning to Fix Noisy Preferences in Diffusion DPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24952) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2604.24952v3) proposes Semi-DPO, a semi-supervised learning method that treats conflicting preference pairs as noisy unlabeled data to improve Diffusion Direct Preference Optimization. The method first trains on a consensus-filtered clean subset, then uses that model as an implicit classifier to generate pseudo-labels for the noisy set through iterative refinement, achieving state-of-the-art alignment results without extra human annotation or explicit reward models. Human visual preferences are inherently multi-dimensional (aesthetics, detail fidelity, semantic alignment), but existing datasets collapse them into single binary winner/loser labels, creating severe label noise that misguides Diffusion DPO. By theoretically showing that this compression produces conflicting gradient signals and then offering a practical fix, Semi-DPO could make preference alignment for text-to-image diffusion models more robust and cheaper to scale. The approach requires no additional human annotation and no explicit reward model during training, relying instead on consensus filtering and pseudo-labeling with iterative refinement. The authors state that code and models will be released at https://github.com/L-CodingSpace/semi-dpo, though the paper is a preprint and results have not yet been peer-reviewed.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a 2023 alignment technique that bypasses explicit reward modeling and reinforcement learning by directly optimizing a policy against human preference pairs using a closed-form loss. Diffusion-DPO adapts this idea to text-to-image diffusion models, aligning generated images with human preferences. Semi-supervised learning is a paradigm that combines a small amount of labeled data with a large amount of unlabeled or imprecisely labeled data, which is exactly the setting Semi-DPO exploits by treating conflicting preference pairs as noisy unlabeled examples.

## [Study Finds Academic AI Evaluations Lag Behind Frontier Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04135) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A large-scale bibliometric audit of 112,303 OpenAlex records (2022-2026) found that the median academic paper evaluates LLMs that are +10.45 ECI points behind the frontier at time of evaluation, and this gap is widening by +4.07 ECI per year. Only 18.4% of full-text papers state an evaluation date, and just 2.2% of abstracts disclose whether reasoning models were tested with reasoning on or off. This quantifies a systematic 'publication elicitation gap' that undermines the reliability of academic AI evaluations, potentially misleading researchers, policymakers, and practitioners who rely on published results. The widening gap suggests that evaluation practices are not keeping pace with rapid model advancement, and the paper proposes a 13-item checklist (VERSIO-AI v1.2) plus enforcement by editors and funders to address it. The study uses the Epoch AI Capabilities Index (ECI), an aggregate LLM capability score, to rank evaluated models against frontier models, with a nominal 95% CI of [+3.75, +4.45] for the annual gap increase. A Bayes-corrected 52.5% of abstracts discuss conclusions in terms of 'AI' as a category rather than specific models, and only 21.2% of full-text articles on reasoning models disclose reasoning on/off status.

## [MoLF Framework Unifies LoRA and Full Fine-Tuning via Gradient Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07111) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.07111v3) empirically compares LoRA and full fine-tuning (FFT) across SQL, Medical QA, and Counterfactual Knowledge tasks using Gemma-3-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen2.5-3B, finding that the better static method depends on the task and model. The authors propose Mixture of LoRA and Full (MoLF) Fine-Tuning, which dynamically routes updates between FFT and LoRA at the optimizer level, plus MoLF-Efficient for memory-constrained settings. The LoRA-versus-FFT choice has been a persistent open question for practitioners adapting LLMs, and MoLF offers a way to avoid committing to one regime upfront. If the reported results hold, it could simplify fine-tuning workflows and improve accuracy across diverse tasks without requiring per-task method selection. MoLF reparameterizes each target linear projection as a superposition of an FFT expert and one or more LoRA experts, using a custom AdamW optimizer that scores experts with the Expected Preconditioned Descent (EPD) statistic and applies Top-K sparse updates while all experts participate in every forward and backward pass. Evaluations show MoLF either improves on or stays within 1.5 percentage points of the better of FFT and LoRA across nine settings, while MoLF-Efficient beats AdaLoRA and AdaMix in eight of nine settings, with gains up to 11.70 points on Fact, 3.13 on Med, and 2.98 on SQL.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation), introduced by Microsoft researchers in 2021, freezes pre-trained model weights and injects small trainable rank-decomposition matrices, greatly reducing trainable parameters and memory costs. Full fine-tuning instead updates all model weights, offering greater representational plasticity but demanding far more compute and GPU memory. Practitioners have long debated which approach yields better downstream performance, since results vary by task and model size.

## [AID: Amortized Inpainting via Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13010) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Amortized Inpainting with Diffusion (AID), a method that keeps a pretrained diffusion backbone frozen and trains a small reusable guidance module offline using a continuous-time actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm. AID reuses this module across masked images without per-instance optimization, and the authors prove that solving an auxiliary Gaussian formulation recovers the optimal deterministic guidance field. AID offers a middle ground between training task-specific models and per-instance optimization, potentially making diffusion-based inpainting faster and more practical for deployment. It consistently improves the quality-speed trade-off over strong fixed-backbone and amortized baselines while adding less than one percent trainable overhead. Experiments are conducted on AFHQv2 and FFHQ under the pixel EDM pipeline and on ImageNet under the latent EDM2 pipeline, across multiple mask types. The method is the first amortized controlled-guidance framework for image inpainting that keeps the pretrained diffusion backbone frozen and provides an exact optimizer-preserving bridge from stochastic actor-critic learning to the deterministic guidance field used at deployment.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Diffusion models generate images by iteratively denoising random noise, and image inpainting uses them to fill in masked regions of an image. Existing approaches either train dedicated task-specific models or adapt a pretrained diffusion model separately for each masked image at deployment, which can be slow or inflexible. Amortized methods aim to train a reusable inference module once so that inference is fast and requires no per-instance optimization. Continuous-time actor-critic reinforcement learning extends temporal-difference learning to continuous time with continuous state and action spaces, and here it is used to learn the guidance module in a fully data-driven manner.

A new arXiv paper (2605.15618v2) presents the first systematic robustness evaluation of four matched-capacity frontier self-supervised video models — V-JEPA 2.1, V-JEPA 2, VideoPrism, and VideoMAEv2 — across five robustness axes: feature discriminability, corruption robustness, fine-grained discrimination, occlusion robustness, and sensitivity to temporal direction. This matters for researchers and practitioners deploying video world models, because only latent prediction yielded near-complete task success in the simulated manipulation environment, remained effective under degraded observations, and transferred to a manipulation task for which the predictor was never trained. The evaluation uses four matched-capacity models and five robustness axes, with the model ordering unchanged when ported from Something-Something-v2 to EGTEA Gaze+; the downstream test pairs each frozen encoder with an identical action-conditioned predictor and planner. The dataset also includes low-cost gold transcripts produced via multi-ASR agreement-guided post-editing and answerability annotations (answerable, ambiguous/needs-clarification, unsupported, not-a-request/noise) to separate intrinsic unanswerability from ASR-induced degradation. It enables researchers to disentangle ASR errors from genuine model limitations, which is critical for building reliable cascaded ASR-to-LLM voice assistants in multilingual settings. The dataset uses multi-ASR agreement-guided post-editing to obtain gold transcripts at low cost, and it introduces a scalable reference-free evaluation method that scores LLM responses from ASR versus gold transcripts using multi-judge LLM scoring. The 2,000-turn test set includes dialect labels for Modern Standard Arabic and four major dialects, and the answerability categories help isolate whether a dislike stems from recognition errors or from ambiguous, out-of-domain, or non-request turns.

At each LLM call the router must select a concrete model from a locked pool, and code and data are available at the project's GitHub repository.

## [SSL Transfer to Time-Series Tasks Is Task-Dependent, Benchmark Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19462) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.19462v2) systematically benchmarks seven representative self-supervised learning methods spanning five SSL paradigms across three time-series tasks—anomaly detection, classification, and forecasting—under parameter- and data-matched budgets. It finds that transfer efficacy is highly task-dependent: SSL yields substantial gains in anomaly detection and effective fine-tuning initializations for classification, but offers limited to no advantage over non-pre-trained controls in forecasting. Self-supervised learning has transformed vision and language, but its value for time series has been unclear and often confounded by inconsistent experimental controls. This benchmark provides rigorous, controlled evidence that practitioners should not assume SSL universally helps, guiding when to invest in pre-training versus simpler baselines. The study also reports that linear probing does not reliably predict fine-tuning performance, that synthetic pre-training is often competitive with real-world corpora, and that scaling encoder depth actually degrades forecasting accuracy. These findings are synthesized into practical evaluation and development guidelines for time-series SSL.

Transfer is typically evaluated either by linear probing, which trains only a simple linear classifier on frozen representations, or by fine-tuning, which updates the entire model. ## [Diffusion-Adaptive Routing Replaces Residual Connections in DiTs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20708) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.20708v3) presents a systematic empirical analysis of cross-layer information flow in Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), identifying three symptoms of standard residual addition: monotonic forward magnitude inflation, sharp backward gradient decay, and pronounced block-wise redundancy. To address these, the authors propose Diffusion-Adaptive Routing (DAR), a drop-in residual replacement that performs learnable, timestep-adaptive, non-incremental aggregation over the history of sublayer outputs. The residual stream is a fundamental architectural component inherited unchanged from the original Transformer, and this work suggests cross-layer information routing is an underexplored design axis in diffusion modeling that operates orthogonally to existing representation-alignment objectives. On ImageNet 256×256, DAR improves SiT-XL/2 by 2.11 FID (7.56 vs. 9.67) and matches baseline converged quality with 8.75× fewer training iterations, which could influence future DiT designs and reduce training costs. ## [Timeflies Jointly Models Future Observability and Values for Irregular Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13571) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2606.13571v2) introduces Timeflies, a unified framework that reformulates time series forecasting as a joint problem of inferring future observability and estimating values, removing the common oracle assumption that future observation timestamps are known in advance. The authors also release the Shadow benchmark, which combines natural missingness from public datasets with real-world industrial data, and propose the Observation-Value Joint Entropy (OVJE) metric to evaluate this coupled predictability. Existing continuous-time models such as Neural ODEs and continuous-time graph networks still implicitly assume future valid observation timestamps are known, which limits their practical relevance in real systems where sensors sleep, transmissions are delayed, and sampling is event-driven. By explicitly modeling whether an observation will occur at all, Timeflies addresses a fundamental limitation for real-world irregular time series forecasting and could improve reliability in industrial monitoring and sensor networks. Timeflies adopts an observation stream and a value stream coupled through three dedicated modules: reliability-aware embedding, observation-guided dependency modeling, and joint prediction. The paper reports that Timeflies consistently outperforms existing methods, and code and dataset are available at https://github.com/ant-intl/Timeflies.

**Background**: Real-world time series are often highly incomplete and irregular due to sensor dormancy, transmission delays, and event-driven sampling, making reliable forecasting fundamentally challenging. Traditional approaches used impute-then-forecast pipelines, while more recent continuous-time models such as Neural ODEs (Chen et al., 2018) parameterize hidden state dynamics with neural networks to handle irregularly sampled data. However, these methods still assume at inference time that the timestamps of future valid observations are known in advance, an implicit oracle assumption that Timeflies aims to remove.

## [FLAPS Unifies Function-Space Regression and PDE Inverse Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22346) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Flow Annealing Posterior Sampling (FLAPS), described as the first function-space posterior sampling framework that unifies stochastic-process regression and PDE inverse problems. Built on pretrained function-space flow-matching priors with a low-rank covariance-preconditioned Langevin correction, it produces coherent posterior samples with well-calibrated uncertainty and outperforms existing functional regression baselines. By bridging stochastic-process regression and scientific inverse problems within a single posterior-sampling framework, FLAPS could simplify how scientific machine learning practitioners handle sparse, noisy observations. Its ability to match or beat diffusion-based posterior samplers while reducing test-time sampling cost makes it attractive for uncertainty quantification in computationally expensive scientific workflows. FLAPS supports variable query discretizations and avoids explicit prior-density evaluation, using a low-rank covariance preconditioner to exploit dominant function-space correlations across discretizations. It was evaluated on Gaussian and non-Gaussian stochastic-process regression benchmarks and diverse PDE inverse problems, though the abstract does not specify the exact datasets or quantitative margins.

Argus introduces a cross-regime benchmark for post-hoc uncertainty quantification (UQ) in single-step executable GUI grounding, evaluating 27 methods across 4 open-weight VLM agents and 4 datasets, plus 8 methods across 3 closed-source vendors. The study finds that UQ rankings transfer well across datasets for a fixed model (Spearman rho up to 0.969) but degrade across model classes and observable interfaces, with cross-tier transfer to closed-source vendors averaging only +0.08. Reliable uncertainty estimates are critical for computer-use agents to reject unsafe actions, calibrate confidence, and define spatial safety regions in safety-critical applications. This benchmark provides the first systematic evidence that UQ rankings are not universally transferable, urging practitioners to rerank UQ methods on target models rather than extrapolate from open-weight results. Hidden-state and density methods (e.g., Mahalanobis, SAPLMA) are the most stable open-weight family, while CoCoA-1MCA, Focus, sampling-based scores, and verbalised self-assessment win in specific regimes. Conformal click regions shrink radii by 40-60% when the plug-in UQ is calibrated, but coverage degrades under calibration-test or interface mismatch.

Researchers introduced ESNN (Equivariant Sheaf Neural Network), an architecture that learns directed, matrix-valued transport between neighboring vector features on graphs while preserving exact Euclidean (E(n)) equivariance. Rather than raising the order of representations, ESNN keeps scalar and vector features first-order and places the added geometric flexibility in the edge transport itself. This offers a complementary route to expressive equivariant message passing without the cost of higher-order representations, which could benefit geometric deep learning tasks such as particle dynamics, mesh simulation, point-cloud classification, and molecular property prediction. It also connects sheaf-theoretic ideas with equivariant graph neural networks, a fast-growing area of research. The paper theoretically characterizes the transport: when relative displacement is the only covariant geometric input, every linear O(n)-equivariant map decomposes into independent radial and tangential components, while learned covariant features enable richer feature-conditioned transformations. It also introduces controlled symmetry relaxation for systems with a preferred ambient direction, which can be prescribed or inferred from data and recovers full E(n)-equivariance when the directional pathway is inactive.

Researchers introduced Homomorphic Encryption-Aware Training (HEAT), a fine-tuning method that makes per-nonlinearity approximation iteration counts learnable so they co-adapt with model weights during training. On encrypted GPT-2 decoding, HEAT reduced iterations by 3.1x, bootstraps by 1.6x, and end-to-end latency by 1.4x while improving decode agreement over the calibrated encrypted baseline. Fully homomorphic encryption lets servers run language models directly on encrypted prompts, but bootstrapping overhead makes inference prohibitively slow. By cutting bootstraps and latency without architectural changes or retraining from scratch, HEAT could help make privacy-preserving encrypted LLM inference more practical for real deployments. Ciphertexts natively support only addition, multiplication, and rotation, and multiplications can be composed only to a bounded depth before a costly bootstrapping operation is required; higher approximation iteration counts buy precision but exhaust depth faster and trigger more bootstraps. The paper further relates iteration count to quantization bit width and, at fixed weights, bounds the gap between the HEAT objective and quantization-aware training.

**Background**: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) is a form of encryption that allows computations to be performed on encrypted data without decrypting it, so a server can process a user's prompt while it remains encrypted. Because ciphertext arithmetic is limited to addition, multiplication, and rotation, every nonlinearity in a neural network must be approximated by an iterative method, and each iteration adds multiplications. When the allowed multiplication depth is exhausted, a bootstrapping operation refreshes the ciphertext, and these bootstraps dominate the latency of encrypted inference.

The paper evaluates spectral normalization in a controlled SO(3)-equivariant model with a matched non-equivariant model, finding that the step size mismatch grows with width in the equivariant model but not in the non-equivariant one. Muon controls effective step size by approximately equalizing the singular values of each momentum matrix, whereas Adam's entrywise normalization only reduces sensitivity to gradient scale without directly controlling per-block effective step size.

## [Order-Invariant Answers, Order-Sensitive Representations in Math Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28442) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.28442v2) studies synthetic multi-step function-composition problems presented under multiple rule orderings that share the same correct answer, and measures a metric called permutation signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) across 16 language models from 1B to 8B parameters. It finds that models solving reordered problems more accurately also represent different rule orderings more distinctly, with layer-averaged permutation SNR positively rank-correlated with accuracy in every setting, reaching Spearman correlations up to 0.86. The result distinguishes answer invariance from representation invariance, suggesting that a model can produce the correct answer while internally encoding equivalent rule orderings in very different ways. This matters for interpretability and reliability research, because it implies that evaluating mathematical reasoning by answer accuracy alone may miss important structure in how models actually process reordered inputs. The study uses synthetic multi-step function-composition tasks and defines permutation SNR to quantify how distinctly ordering patterns are represented relative to variation across problem instances. The correlation is measured on layer-averaged SNR across 16 models ranging from 1B to 8B parameters, so the finding is empirical and correlational rather than a causal claim about training dynamics.

**Background**: Language models are known to be sensitive to input order, a problem often called order bias or positional bias, and prior work has proposed permutation-invariant architectures and diagnostics to enforce consistent responses. Function composition is the mathematical operation of applying one function to the result of another, and multi-step composition problems require chaining several such operations in sequence. Signal-to-noise ratio is a general measure of how strong a target signal is relative to background variation, and here it is adapted to measure how strongly a model's internal representations encode rule ordering.

## [CrossSafe: Cross-Embodiment Latent Safety Filters for Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28984) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CrossSafe proposes an embodiment-conditioned safety filter that shares a Hamilton-Jacobi reachability-based value function and safety-maximizing policy across heterogeneous robots, performing reachability analysis directly in a morphology-aware latent space. Trained jointly across five manipulation tasks and four bimanual embodiments, a single policy achieves zero-shot generalization to a held-out embodiment and reduces the nominal policy's collision rate. As generalist vision-language-action policies increasingly operate in a shared end-effector action space, safety enforcement has become a bottleneck because the same abstract action can be safe for one robot and unsafe for another. CrossSafe shows that safety reasoning can be shared across embodiments while remaining conditioned on morphology, which could make generalist manipulation policies safer to deploy across diverse hardware. The method uses a morphology-aware latent representation of the robot and its environment so that learned safety concepts generalize across embodiments while remaining explicitly conditioned on each robot's morphology and kinematics. Results also show that training with more embodiments improves generalization, though the evaluation is limited to five bimanual embodiments and five whole-body collision-avoidance manipulation tasks.

## [The Sequential Price of Continual Learning: A Theoretical Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29674) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.29674v2) theoretically quantifies the 'sequential price'—the extra loss incurred by sequential task updates in continual learning—using an overparameterized linear-regression model with i.i.d. task sampling. It proves that distribution-level forgetting and population loss converge to the same stationary limit, and analyzes fixed-strength elastic weight consolidation (EWC) under general task curvatures. This work gives the continual learning community a rigorous theoretical handle on why sequential training is inherently costly and how much EWC can mitigate that cost, potentially guiding the design of better regularization-based methods. It matters for researchers and practitioners who need principled trade-offs between plasticity and stability in lifelong learning systems. In more homogeneous task geometries, the sequential price equals the intrinsic loss asymptotically attained by joint training, making the total loss twice as large; under strong EWC regularization, the price decays inversely with EWC strength while the mean-square coupling horizon grows proportionally. Experiments on Jester and Rotated MNIST support the predicted sequential price and its reduction by EWC, with quantitative agreement on real-world tasks satisfying the theory's assumptions and qualitative agreement under nonlinear finite-step training.

**Background**: Continual learning aims to train models on a sequence of tasks without forgetting earlier ones, a challenge known as catastrophic forgetting. Elastic weight consolidation (EWC) is a popular regularization method that penalizes changes to parameters important for previous tasks, using the Fisher information matrix to estimate importance. This paper abstracts the problem into an overparameterized linear-regression setting to derive exact theoretical limits on the performance cost of sequential updates.

## [FlashForward Reuses In-Flight KV Cache to Speed Up Autoregressive Video Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32540) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new paper introduces FlashForward, a method that directly reuses the in-flight key-value (KV) cache computed during each denoising forward of the current chunk, eliminating the extra cache-update-only forwards that prior autoregressive video diffusion methods required. With up to four GPUs, it runs 1.16–1.69x faster than HiAR and 1.42–2.92x faster than Self-Forcing for 16 FPS videos of 20 seconds or longer across 1.3B and 14B backbone scales at 480p and 720p. Long-form video generation with autoregressive diffusion is bottlenecked by the growing KV cache and the redundant forwards used to maintain it, so removing those forwards directly improves inference speed and makes real-time or interactive video synthesis more feasible. The method also enables concurrent processing of different chunks across GPUs, pointing toward more parallel and deployable long-video generation pipelines. Because the reused cache is stage-matched and therefore noisy, FlashForward adds sparse auxiliary clean anchor latents generated before the corresponding region, combining coarse long-range structural guidance from clean anchors with dense recent history from the stage-matched cache. On VBench, the 1.3B model at 480p achieves higher scores and remains stable at 20s, 35s, and 65s durations.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Autoregressive video diffusion generates long videos by splitting them into temporal chunks and denoising each chunk through a short sequence of stages, using a key-value (KV) cache to remember previously generated content. Prior methods rebuilt a clean or less-noisy KV cache with extra forwards that did not advance the output latent, which added significant compute overhead. FlashForward instead exploits the fact that every denoising forward already computes the KV of the current chunk, and pairs this noisy stage-matched history with sparse clean anchors to prevent appearance and motion drift.

The paper introduces Elastic Forcing, a post-training framework that learns the rollout distribution directly from reference videos by minimizing maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) in frozen self-supervised video representation spaces, eliminating both the bidirectional diffusion teacher and online fake-score model used in Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD). Using the same architecture and initialization as Self-Forcing, the 1.3B model improves the VBench Total score from 83.80 to 84.64 while retaining 17 FPS, and removing auxiliary score models enables 14B post-training on eight H200 GPUs. It also opens the door to learning new visual styles, semantic concepts, and spatial priors directly from reference videos without a target-specific diffusion teacher, potentially broadening the applicability of autoregressive video models. The method uses a hybrid Nyström–Monte Carlo estimator to balance approximation bias and sampling variance, combined with memory-efficient replay and gradient subsampling to make the objective practical. The approach is evaluated on a 1.3B model with the same architecture and initialization as Self-Forcing, achieving a VBench improvement while maintaining 17 FPS inference.

The analysis shows that relational preservation and marginal calibration impose non-redundant constraints, and connects finite-candidate planning stability to relational distortion, latent-scale mismatch, and prediction error. Diagnostics further show stronger novelty-related structure in the planning latent, improved marginal calibration, and lower multi-step prediction error.

The target theorem was withheld from the agent's task instructions, and the saved research log records rejected geometric hypotheses and a cubic fitted to polygon sides; discovery-set diagonals served only as an out-of-fit consistency check rather than a fully held-out test, and a separate one-configuration run reported insufficient evidence for invariance. ## [Concept-Grounded Attention Injects Versioned Concept Graphs into Transformer Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38684) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The arXiv preprint introduces the Concept Lifecycle Model (CLM), which represents concepts as persistent, graph-grounded, temporally versioned entities with explicit provenance and epistemic status, and Concept-Grounded Attention (CGA), which injects concept-graph structure into transformer computation via graph-biased self-attention (Form A) and gated cross-attention over concept nodes (Form B). Controlled experiments on 200 MuSiQue and HotpotQA questions show that concept-graph retrieval recovers explicit multi-hop paths but does not improve evidence recall, and that Form A's apparent attention steering disappears under disabled-mechanism controls. The work argues that temporal validity and epistemic status should be made explicit in knowledge-grounded NLP systems, since explicit temporal representation improved LongMemEval answer accuracy by 13 to 25 points across generators up to 122B parameters, and protocol-derived epistemic status cut unsupported assertions from 28% to 0.1% in a fine-tuned small model. It also serves as a methodological warning that graph-attention diagnostics are uninformative without disabled-mechanism controls, which matters for researchers evaluating knowledge injection techniques. Form A showed 2.76 times more attention on gold than distractor concepts, but the same ratio occurred when Form A was disabled, the learned bias was negligible, and no answers changed; an identity-preserving Form B improved F1 from 0.188 to 0.221, yet control concepts yielded 0.213, indicating most of the gain reflects added capacity. On LongMemEval, simplified CLM version resolution performed similarly to dated serialization because concept identity is not established reliably, and epistemic-status gains were measured on a synthetic source-independence task.

## [Strict vs Advisory Token Budget Stopping in Test-Time Math Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38699) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38699) measures how a cumulative token cap falling inside a mathematical derivation affects accuracy, using paired offline replays of 19,200 public traces across 120 AIME, BrUMO and HMMT problems with a fixed 16-attempt cap and answer selection blind to correctness labels. It finds that at the 4k cap, most advisory accuracy gains come from replacing abstention with a correct answer, and that advisory 4k in low configuration beats strict 8k at comparable mean completion cost. This work matters for anyone deploying test-time reasoning systems with hard token budgets, because it shows that the choice between strict and advisory stopping changes accuracy, abstention behavior, and realized cost in ways that same-cap comparisons hide. It argues that budget curves should jointly report the cap, realized cost, eligible candidates, stopping rule and selector information, which could reshape how inference efficiency is benchmarked. The study uses two archive configurations of one model and finds that increased candidate coverage does not guarantee higher answer accuracy — a log-probability selector loses accuracy as coverage rises, even after a source-grade consistency repair, and same-cap majority-accuracy differences shrink below 1.3 percentage points at 32k. The authors caution that aggregate comparisons do not establish equal-compute superiority or accuracy equivalence, and the abstract is truncated.

A new arXiv paper analyzes JEV 1.13 and three open KEV models, identifying an "ordinal scale-utilization bias" where models underuse the provided decision scale. On ANLI, JEV assigned 38.8% of predictions and 51.3% of errors to Neutral despite 74.95% accuracy, and across 36 ordinal datasets decisions used only 67–76% of effective gold support versus 87–102% on nominal tasks. The finding shows the compression is learned and can be mitigated by targeted post-training, which could improve model calibration and trustworthiness in evaluation pipelines. BA-LoRA post-training raised gold-relative utilization from roughly 47% to 86% on eight supervised scales at both KEV sizes, demonstrating the compression is modifiable rather than an architectural limit.
