## [Reserve-C4B: Reserve-Aware Contrast Certificates for Conservative Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39106) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Reserve-C4B, a conservative bandit algorithm built around the baseline-relative contrast itself rather than separately bounding candidate and baseline rewards. It uses a shared confidence set to derive an exact expression for the avoidable double-charging penalty, plus a reserve ledger and a prefix-refresh extension that recertifies accumulated decisions under the current confidence set without discarding previously certified credit. Conservative bandits are used when a system must explore new strategies while keeping performance above an incumbent baseline, such as in revenue management or safe online recommendation. By removing the double-counting of shared estimation error, Reserve-C4B can reduce unnecessary fallback to the baseline, making conservative exploration less wasteful while still satisfying performance constraints with high probability. For linear rewards, the method uses self-normalized confidence sets that remain simultaneously valid over time and over adaptively generated candidates, yielding a policy that satisfies a conditional-mean performance constraint with high probability. Reproducible experiments isolate certificate coupling, prefix refresh, and historical information, showing large reductions in baseline fallback while also exposing the limitations of frozen certificates.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Conservative bandits are a variant of the multi-armed bandit problem in which a learning agent must improve on an incumbent policy while never letting cumulative performance fall below a prescribed baseline budget. In the classic formulation, the baseline is assumed known, but in many real settings the baseline itself must be estimated from data, which introduces uncertainty. Naively bounding the candidate and the baseline separately can charge the same estimation error twice, making the algorithm overly conservative and causing it to fall back to the baseline more often than necessary.

## [Scoping Review Questions Component-Replacement Evidence in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39989) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A critical scoping review of 348 studies, examining 90 comparison records from 40 included studies, argues that component-replacement comparisons in LLM agents cannot by themselves establish that better local decisions explain task-level gains. It derives eight claim-specific reporting items to separate a replacement's task-level benefit from the contribution of local decision quality. As LLM agent research increasingly swaps out components such as detectors, retrievers, or termination policies, this review warns that common evaluation practices may over-attribute task-level improvements to local decision quality. It offers the agent-evaluation community concrete reporting criteria to make causal claims more defensible. Of 222 studies reporting local decision metrics, 142 also report measured task endpoints and 49 report proxies, but these counts only show co-reporting, not matched comparisons. Case analyses such as Outcome Monitors, First-chunk selection, and Evidence-Carrying Termination show that gains in local and task metrics do not establish that better local decisions caused the task-level gain.

**Background**: LLM agents are systems in which a language model plans and acts over multiple steps, using tools, memory, and control logic to complete tasks. Turbo Harness introduces a framework that takes a globally optimized agent harness and adapts it to each individual task instance by recycling artifacts from the original optimization run into a structured playbook. A trained harness editor then uses that playbook plus the instance to generate instance-specific patches, producing a tailored harness for the execution model at inference time. Existing harness optimization methods produce one global harness applied uniformly to all tasks, which may be suboptimal for individual instances; instance-adaptive harnessing could improve agent reliability on long-horizon and interactive tasks. The framework claims three advantages, with instance-adaptive harnessing offering more flexibility than a single global harness and consistently improving task performance. Experiments report that Turbo Harness outperforms existing harness optimization baselines across seven benchmarks covering interactive agent tasks, software engineering, and long-horizon terminal tasks, though the abstract is truncated and lacks detailed numbers or comparisons.

## [Derandomizing Dense Binary Hypervector Codebooks for Quantized Scalars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38471) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (arXiv:2609.38471) develops a transition-based derandomization framework for dense binary scalar codebooks in hyperdimensional computing, covering two target-similarity families where similarity decays exponentially or linearly with level separation. The framework separates the target similarity law, the derandomization variant, and the concrete generator construction, and derives exact finite-dimensional expressions for bias, variance, and root-mean-square error, validated by simulations across dimensions, quantization ranges, and generator constructions. This work matters because randomized scalar codebook constructions deviate from their intended similarity profiles at finite dimensionality due to sampling noise, random-start imbalance, update-count fluctuations, component dependence, and finite-capacity effects, which can degrade the reliability of hyperdimensional computing and vector symbolic architectures. By providing practical guidance for choosing codebook generators that more closely match a desired similarity law under finite-dimensional and hardware-relevant constraints, it could improve the accuracy and predictability of HDC/VSA systems used in emerging hardware. The framework formalizes derandomization variants that separately constrain initial Hamming weight, update-count variability, and update balance, thereby controlling distinct sources of finite-dimensional error. For each similarity family and variant, the authors derive the induced mean similarity, identify realization-wise and mean target-matching regimes, and show through simulations how each constraint removes or reduces a specific source of similarity mismatch.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC), also known as vector symbolic architectures (VSA), is a neuro-inspired computational framework that represents information as very high-dimensional vectors called hypervectors, often with thousands of components. In HDC/VSA, quantized scalar levels are commonly encoded as dense binary codebooks whose pairwise similarity is designed to follow a prescribed function of scalar separation. Derandomization is the process of replacing randomized algorithmic choices with deterministic ones to eliminate sampling variability and improve reproducibility. At finite dimensionality, randomized codebook constructions suffer from sampling noise and other effects that cause the realized similarity to deviate from the target, motivating deterministic construction methods.

## [Seed-Q: Security-Enhanced Seed-Based Weight Quantization for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38477) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers introduced Seed-Q, a security-enhanced, sensitivity-aware seed-based weight compression framework for large language models that combines lightweight LFSR-based weight generation with non-uniform bit allocation. Experiments show Seed-Q matches the 4-bit perplexity of SeedLM with fewer bits, and at the same 4 bits/weight it reduces both perplexity degradation and zero-shot accuracy loss, while also achieving high security against bit-flip attacks and modest ASIC hardware overhead. As LLMs grow larger, storage, memory-bandwidth and energy costs dominate deployment, so compression methods that preserve accuracy are highly valuable. Seed-Q's combination of better compression, built-in detection of bit-flip attacks, and low hardware overhead could make seed-based compression more practical for secure and efficient LLM inference. The non-uniform bit allocation requires no side-information: the decoder deterministically reconstructs the bit-allocation schedule, with no rung depending on decoded weights, so no per-block metadata or calibration data is needed while the baseline coding rate is preserved. Security comes from the fact that a bit corruption affects multiple reconstructed weights, amplifying its impact and making attacks easier to detect.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Seed-based compression encodes blocks of neural network weights as seeds fed into a pseudo-random generator, such as a Linear Feedback Shift Register (LFSR), which regenerates the weights at inference time; Apple's SeedLM is a well-known example of this approach. Prior seed-based methods treat all weights uniformly, ignoring that some weights are more sensitive to quantization error than others, and non-uniform bit allocation has separately been shown to outperform uniform allocation at the same storage budget. Seed-Q combines these ideas while adding a security dimension against bit-flip attacks on model parameters.

## [Study Reconciles Conflicting Results on Concept Bottleneck Model Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38625) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces a generator-based evaluation framework that systematically compares standard classifiers and Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) under two perturbation regimes: continuous geometric perturbations in latent space and discrete semantic interventions in concept space. Using both empirical sensitivity metrics and certified robustness via randomized smoothing, the authors show that concept bottlenecks do not uniformly improve robustness but instead redistribute sensitivity across perturbation spaces and model families. The findings clarify why prior studies reported mixed and contradictory results about CBM robustness, and they argue that interpretability and robustness are distinct objectives rather than inherently linked. This matters for researchers and practitioners building interpretable models, since it suggests that adding a concept bottleneck should not be assumed to confer adversarial robustness. The framework evaluates robustness both empirically, via prediction and concept-level sensitivity metrics, and certifiably, using randomized smoothing in latent and concept spaces. The authors further analyze how task conditions such as class semantic similarity and concept vocabulary size affect robustness, revealing a nuanced interpretability-robustness trade-off that depends critically on the perturbation regime and task structure.

**Background**: Concept Bottleneck Models are inherently interpretable architectures that first predict a set of human-understandable concepts from the input, then use those concepts to make the final prediction, allowing humans to inspect and even correct intermediate concept values. Randomized smoothing is a certifiable defense that converts any base classifier into a robust majority-vote classifier by injecting controlled random noise, yielding certified robustness guarantees. Prior work on CBM robustness has produced conflicting conclusions, which this paper attributes to conflating different robustness notions and perturbation regimes.

The paper introduces signal-routed temperature scaling (SRTS-BCE), a 10-parameter, argmax-preserving calibrator that cross-fits a correctness-risk score over six logit statistics and fits one top-label-BCE temperature per K=3 risk groups, recovering TvA-TS as its K=1 limit. This work reframes post-hoc calibrator capacity as a finite-sample statistical design choice rather than a purely architectural one, showing that the preferred level of adaptivity shifts with the amount of available calibration data. SRTS-BCE is argmax-preserving, so it does not change the model's predicted class labels, only its confidence estimates. The small-budget advantage is supported by a seed-to-draw hierarchical interval that excludes zero, but the flagship comparison against the scalar TvA-TS remains only directional, and a protocol-frozen Tiny-ImageNet follow-up shows a budget-dependent ranking reversal on Swin-T.

## [Structured Criteria Extraction vs. Chain-of-Thought for LLM Depression Rating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39049) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv study compares structured clinical criteria extraction against chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting for LLM-based depression severity rating across two Reddit corpora, three LLMs (9B to frontier scale), and two questionnaires (PHQ-9, BDI-II), using quadratic weighted kappa as the agreement metric. The study finds that criteria extraction only beats CoT on one corpus for frontier models when decision thresholds are fitted on labeled data, and even then the gain is not statistically significant; with a priori thresholds, extraction shows no gain at all. This work matters for clinical NLP and LLM evaluation because it challenges the assumption that more auditable structured criteria extraction inherently improves model performance, showing that apparent gains may be a calibration artifact rather than a genuine reasoning advantage. It also warns that higher ordinal agreement does not guarantee better detection of severe depression cases, which is critical for any real-world mental health screening application. The 9B model behaves differently on a corpus from depression communities, labeling most posts as severe whether prompted directly or with CoT, while the a priori rule beats both without labels. PHQ-9 criteria extraction misses most severe posts, and moving from direct prompting to CoT and then to extraction increases misses in nearly all comparisons; on the primary corpus, a model using that dataset's own features (including word counts) is not significantly different from frontier criteria extraction under the a priori rule.

## [Time-Aware BORF Extends Interpretable Classification to Irregular Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39268) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.39268) extends the Bag-Of-Receptive-Fields (BORF) transform to irregular time series by introducing a time-weighted normalization scheme that weights each observation proportionally to its time delta. The authors derive an efficient sliding-window recurrence for the time-weighted standard deviation, preserving BORF's linear time complexity, and benchmark the method against state-of-the-art irregular time series classifiers on the PYRREGULAR repository. Irregular time series are ubiquitous in healthcare, mobility, and environmental monitoring, yet interpretable classifiers for this setting remain limited; most existing methods rely on imputation that obscures temporal structure or on opaque neural architectures. By avoiding imputation while retaining human-interpretable explanations, this work could make high-stakes domains such as clinical monitoring more trustworthy and easier to audit. The core technical contribution is a time-weighted normalization in which each observation's contribution scales with its associated time delta, making pattern extraction sensitive to the actual temporal distribution of samples rather than only their index position. The authors derive a sliding-window recurrence for the time-weighted standard deviation so that the transform retains BORF's linear time complexity, and they report competitive classification performance on PYRREGULAR datasets without imputation.

## [WinoTS Uses Wavelet Self-Distillation for Time Series Pre-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39337) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.39337) introduces WinoTS, an invariance-based self-distillation pre-training paradigm that uses time-frequency wavelet augmentations to create multi-scale structural views of temporal signals. The authors report that WinoTS outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in long-term forecasting, cross-domain zero-shot transfer, and unsupervised anomaly detection, with linear probing on frozen representations often surpassing fully supervised models trained from scratch. Most time series pre-training today relies on next-token prediction or reconstruction, which can waste capacity on high-frequency point-wise noise; WinoTS offers a principled alternative by adapting the successful invariance-based self-distillation recipe from computer vision to temporal data. If the results hold, it could shift how practitioners build foundation models for forecasting, transfer, and anomaly detection across domains such as energy, finance, and industrial monitoring. The core idea is that spatial augmentations like cropping can shift the timing of repeating cycles or distort signals, while simple jittering provides limited variation, so WinoTS instead uses time-frequency transformations to build views without distorting underlying dynamics. Systematic ablations show the framework is architecture-agnostic and yields gains across different time series backbones.

A new arXiv preprint (2609.39342) extends the Maximum Occupancy Principle (MOP) to partially observable environments and introduces a Bellman reformulation of Expected Free Energy within the Active Inference framework, both incorporating belief-based inference over hidden states. The Bellman formulation enables tractable offline computation via value iteration over the full belief-state space, and experiments with uncertain food sources show MOP agents switch between goal-directed food seeking and exploration based on energy and belief state. This work bridges intrinsic motivation methods like MOP with the principled Active Inference framework, potentially enabling more adaptive agents in noisy, uncertain environments relevant to reinforcement learning and neuroscience. It also provides a computationally tractable route for offline planning in belief spaces, which could influence future research on exploration and goal-directed behavior. The Bellman reformulation allows value iteration over the full belief-state space, making offline computation tractable, though the experiments are limited to minimal settings with uncertain food sources. MOP agents exhibit switching between food-seeking and exploration depending on energy and belief state, whereas Active Inference agents mostly stay around a single food source, and Empowerment is shown to be qualitatively similar to Active Inference.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Active Inference is a normative framework for Bayes-optimal behavior and cognition, where agents act to minimize expected free energy by balancing goal-directed and epistemic drives. The Maximum Occupancy Principle (MOP) is an intrinsic motivation approach proposing that agents maximize occupancy over future paths of states and actions, without explicit preferences or epistemic targets, yet producing rich exploratory and goal-directed behavior. Bellman equations are recursive formulations from dynamic programming that break an optimization problem into simpler subproblems, commonly used in reinforcement learning for value iteration. This paper combines these ideas to handle partially observable environments where agents must infer hidden states.

It compares Monte Carlo Dropout (MCD), Deep Ensembles (DE), and Monte Carlo Deep Ensembles (MCDE), analyzing predictive, aleatoric, and epistemic uncertainty across tasks. Trustworthy AI in high-stakes medical imaging requires reliable uncertainty estimates, and this task-aware evaluation offers practical guidance for developing safer glioma diagnostic systems. It highlights that no single UQ method dominates across tasks, which matters for clinicians and researchers choosing methods for multi-task medical AI. Uncertainty estimates supported meaningful error detection, but calibration depended on the dropout rate, with moderate rates yielding the most reliable probabilities. Uncertainty decomposition provided task-dependent interpretability but did not consistently improve error detection over predictive uncertainty alone, and the composite trust score did not consistently outperform classification uncertainty for selective prediction.

## [Abductive Candidate Retention Balances Supervision for Abductive Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39561) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2609.39561) introduces Abductive Candidate Retention (ACR), a method that selects a subset of abductive explanations rather than picking a single candidate or weighting all candidates. ACR uses a coordinate-level supervision error bound based on retained uncertainty, discarded model mass, and model mismatch, and greedily accepts a candidate when its recovered mass exceeds the increase in retained uncertainty. Abductive learning sits at the intersection of neural perception and symbolic reasoning, where multiple valid explanations can assign conflicting pseudo-labels to the same inputs. ACR offers a principled way to retain informative candidates, potentially improving concept accuracy over single-candidate baselines and prior methods like A3BL in aggregated mod-addition settings. The theoretical bound decomposes supervision error into retained uncertainty, discarded model mass, and model mismatch; for a fixed model and training pair, only the first two terms depend on the retained set. Experiments show ACR improves concept accuracy over single-candidate baselines and A3BL in most evaluated aggregated mod-addition settings, and ablations support jointly using uncertainty and posterior mass.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Abductive learning (ABL) integrates machine learning with logical reasoning in a loop: a perception model predicts symbolic concept labels from raw inputs, abduction uses domain knowledge to revise those labels, and the revised labels are fed back for retraining. Because abduction is nondeterministic, multiple valid explanations can produce conflicting pseudo-labels for the same input, which can destabilize training. Pseudo-labeling is a common semi-supervised technique where model-generated labels supervise further training, and neurosymbolic AI aims to combine neural networks with symbolic reasoning for more reliable and interpretable systems.

The results show that performing data assimilation in the intermediate w-space yields better history matching than the traditional z-space, because w-space is more linear and disentangled, keeping updated vectors close to realistic geological patterns. The advantage of w-space is attributed to ESMDA's linear updates, which interact better with the more disentangled w-space than with the highly entangled z-space, and the results were validated with standard geostatistical and history-matching metrics.

## [SEPAL Uses Private Actor-Critic Teams and Answer-Level Voting for LLM Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39645) ⭐️ 6.0/10

SEPAL introduces three private Actor-Critic teams, each trained for a distinct reasoning objective—direct reasoning, evidence grounding, and verification—and combines only their final answers via majority voting. Across five open-weight backbones and five question-answering benchmarks, it improves mean accuracy by 1.81 percentage points over a matched single Actor-Critic pair, with gains on all five backbones. The work addresses a key failure mode in multi-agent LLM collaboration: shared discussion can couple error correction with exposure to the same mistakes, eroding the diversity that voting relies on. By keeping reasoning histories separate until the final decision, SEPAL offers a more reliable way to combine LLM deliberation with ensemble-style voting, which could influence how multi-agent QA systems are designed. SEPAL assigns role-specific training so the teams have different reasoning objectives beyond mere sampling variation, and each Critic guides revisions only within its own team to prevent feedback from carrying errors across candidates. After revision ends, majority voting combines only the final answers, keeping reasoning histories separate until the decision; code is available at https://github.com/zhansan114514/SEPAL.

**Background**: Actor-Critic is a reinforcement learning framework in which an Actor selects actions and a Critic estimates their value to guide learning. ## [TRACE: Lightweight Trajectory Selection for Parallel Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39912) ⭐️ 6.0/10

TRACE (Trajectory Ranking with Aggregated Cross-Rollout Evidence) is a lightweight learned selector that ranks completed search trajectories by aggregating evidence across parallel rollouts, rather than relying on final-answer voting. On Qwen2.5-14B Base/SFT WebQA pools it reaches 45.2/49.2% EM at K=16, beating the strongest Qwen3-32B generative aggregators (43.9/48.0%), and on long-horizon FRAMES, GAIA, and BrowseComp it achieves 78.6% average accuracy, 3.1 points above majority voting. Parallel search agents often generate a correct answer that final-answer voting fails to select, so a better consolidation stage directly improves reliability without extra search or autoregressive aggregation. Because one selector per search setting transfers across rollout policies and agent backbones, TRACE offers an efficient alternative to heavyweight generative aggregation for test-time scaling of search agents. TRACE preserves individual query and evidence occurrences, links rollouts through shared content or document identity, and propagates information across these relations, so each candidate answer reads its own trajectory state plus evidence from related rollouts while preserving retrieval provenance. It is trained with answer-level supervision over frozen text embeddings, returns an existing answer without additional search, and achieves at least 10x higher processing throughput than SolAgg, SummAgg, and AggAgent across all seven WebQA benchmarks; notably, with only 8 rollouts it comes within 0.4 points of majority voting over 64 on Base WebQA pools.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Parallel search agents scale test-time compute by running many independent search rollouts for the same question, then consolidating their outputs into one answer. The standard consolidation method is majority voting over final answers, but it discards the intermediate search evidence each rollout gathered, so a correct answer supported by strong evidence can lose to a more frequent but weaker one. Trajectory selection reframes consolidation as ranking whole trajectories rather than counting answer strings, and prior generative aggregators that summarize or merge rollouts are accurate but computationally heavy.

The paper proposes the Cluster Attention Neural Operator (CANO), which reformulates attention through a novel cross-attention mechanism that dynamically clusters queries while preserving full-resolution keys and values. This avoids the slice-compression loss and weight-sharing limits of Transolver, and CANO reportedly achieves state-of-the-art performance on canonical PDE benchmarks including Navier-Stokes, Airfoil, Plasticity, Pipe Turbulence, and Composites. Parametric PDE simulation is a bottleneck in engineering design, and neural operators promise orders-of-magnitude speedups; CANO's ability to keep global interactions fast while preserving fine spatial detail could make Transformer-style operators more practical for high-fidelity, multi-query design workflows. It also matters for scientific machine learning because it directly targets the quadratic-attention cost that limits Transformer-based operators on large meshes. CANO uses cross-attention to dynamically cluster queries while keeping full-resolution keys and values, which removes the slice compression and shared-weight constraints of Transolver. The paper evaluates the model on fluid and solid dynamics, irregular unstructured geometries, and long-term temporal rollouts, reporting lower errors than baselines along with strong geometric adaptability and temporal consistency.

**Background**: Parametric PDEs describe physical systems whose behavior depends on parameters such as material properties or flow conditions, and traditional solvers must recompute the solution for every new parameter set. ## [CAS II: Symmetric Partitions as Kolmogorov Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40290) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper develops algorithmic statistics over symmetric partitions — the orbit partitions of groups acting on binary strings — using the Galois connection between subgroups and partitions to define a structure function and a symmetric sophistication measure. It shows that for the full symmetric group every partition is symmetric and cells recover all Kolmogorov models, while for GL(n,2) the cells are exactly the linearly homogeneous sets, and it gives coordinates on permutation groups via a Burnside ring type plus a placement. This connects algorithmic information theory with group theory, offering a new lens on which regularities of a string are genuinely symmetric and thus potentially learnable by symmetry-restricted hypothesis classes. It matters for researchers studying model selection, minimum description length, and the limits of search over structured hypothesis spaces. For nonzero x, the linear-symmetry structure function lies in a band between the sufficiency line and the trivial bound, and both edges are attained, meaning there exist stochastic normal strings whose simple structure is invisible to linear symmetry. The maximal gap theorem further shows that any space of symmetry hypotheses small enough to search is small enough to miss simple structure.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 1, 04:00

**Background**: Algorithmic statistics explains a binary string x by finding a finite set (a model) containing it, and Kolmogorov's structure function records the smallest such model at each level of complexity; Vereshchagin's strong models are those computable from the data by a total algorithm, essentially the cells of simple partitions. A Galois connection is a correspondence between two partially ordered sets, here between subgroups and partitions, which yields a lattice of symmetric partitions with canonical certificates and costs. Kolmogorov complexity measures the length of the shortest program that outputs a string, and sophistication measures how much of a string's structure is captured by a simple model.

KMAS constructs hard negatives via updated relation embeddings rather than random entity replacement, and its training schedule uses a warmup followed by linear increase then linear decrease of the hard-negative ratio to align with the model's evolving capability. TIDE treats memory as a capacity-constrained population of experiences, using temporal and semantic credit assignment to estimate contextual fitness and responsibility credit to distribute outcome signals according to which memories were referenced during generation. The paper introduces OLAS (Optimal Labeler Assignment and Sampling), an active learning framework that explicitly models label noise as a function of both labeler accuracy and model uncertainty. It develops two tractable optimization formulations—one for assigning samples to labelers to minimize worst-case noise, and another for selecting samples while controlling overall label noise—with closed-form solutions under mild conditions, and demonstrates top or near-top accuracy on benchmark datasets and a real-world warranty claim classification task using only a single label per sample. This work addresses a critical gap in active learning: most existing strategies assume perfect oracles, but real-world labeling often involves noisy annotators of varying expertise. The noise model ε(a,e) depends on labeler accuracy and sample entropy, and the framework provides a closed-form optimal labeler assignment policy plus a joint sampling-and-assignment optimization that respects a noise bound β. Empirical results show OLAS achieves the highest or near-highest classification accuracy among existing AL strategies across most settings, using only a single label per sample, though the approach assumes access to labeler accuracy estimates and may face scalability challenges in large-scale settings.

A new arXiv paper (2608.26410v3) studies whether envy-freeness and equitability can be simultaneously satisfied in fair division. For normalized binary goods, it gives a polynomial-time algorithm computing an EF1+EQ1 allocation for at most seven agents, but constructs a normalized instance with more agents where no such allocation exists; in sharp contrast, binary chores admit the stronger EFX+EQX guarantee for any number of agents, even without normalization. This work sharpens the boundary between what is achievable for goods versus chores, showing that two fundamentally different fairness notions can coexist under strong guarantees in the chores setting while failing for goods. It matters for algorithmic game theory and computational social choice researchers designing fair allocation mechanisms, and it opens a new direction on cross-notion ex-ante and ex-post guarantees. The positive result for goods requires normalization and is limited to at most seven agents, while the impossibility construction uses a larger number of agents, so the exact threshold remains a sharp open boundary. The chores result is stronger (EFX+EQX) and holds for any number of agents without normalization, and the paper also initiates the study of whether randomized allocations can provide ex-ante guarantees for one notion while preserving ex-post guarantees for another.

## [Dec-BFTRL Achieves Square-Root Regret for Decentralized Online Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30271) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Dec-BFTRL (Decentralized Barrier Follow-the-Regularized-Leader), a decentralized online optimization algorithm that achieves expected network-aggregate regret of Õ(√T) for upper-linearizable payoffs under efficient separation access. Each agent maps an internal iterate to a feasible action via an approximate gauge projection, communicates only a cumulative surrogate-gradient dual state, and uses a local HybridNewton procedure, with wrapper instantiations covering four up-concave or DR-submodular maximization problems. This is a solid theoretical contribution to decentralized online optimization, showing that square-root regret is attainable for upper-linearizable payoffs even when agents only have separation access to the action set. It extends regret guarantees to continuous diminishing-return submodular maximization, a class of non-convex problems relevant to multi-agent learning and resource allocation. Over T rounds, each agent uses T neighbor-mixing steps and Õ(T) separation-oracle calls, and the analysis relies on an upper-linearizable function class with structural parameters alpha and beta plus an action map h. The approach requires an approximate gauge projection and a HybridNewton subroutine, so practical efficiency depends on the cost of these local computations.

**Background**: Decentralized online optimization studies settings where multiple agents repeatedly choose actions and only communicate with neighbors in a network, aiming to minimize regret relative to the best fixed action in hindsight. Upper-linearizable payoffs are a broad function class that can be bounded above by linear functions, which makes regret analysis tractable. Continuous DR-submodular functions satisfy a diminishing-returns condition and form a subclass of continuous submodular functions that can often be optimized efficiently despite non-convexity. Separation access means the feasible action set is not given explicitly but can be queried through a separation oracle that returns a violated constraint when a point is infeasible.

After the actual observation arrives, the framework reconstructs alternative judgments from the base forecast's residual, evaluates them by their resulting adjustments, and retains the best-performing decision as validated experience for future forecasts.
